## Results

Elevated actin-binding related genes promote tip cell formation and tumor neovascularization
To investigate the cytoskeletal changes in TECs, we analyzed the expression of genes encoding actin-binding proteins using publicly available single-cell RNA sequencing (scRNA-seq) data of human lung TECs and normal ECs (NECs) (E-MTAB-6308)5. Compared with NECs, 70 actin-binding-related genes were upregulated, including MYO1B, CXCR4, and SYNPO, while 11 genes were downregulated, including SLC6A4 and S100A4 (Fig. 1a, Supplementary Fig. 1a). This finding suggests abnormalities in the TEC cytoskeleton that promote cell migration. Among these genes, we found that the cytoskeleton-related PDLIM family proteins, including PDLIM1, PDLIM7, and PDLIM5, were highly expressed in TECs, indicating an important role for PDLIM family proteins in TECs. PDLIM proteins are known for their roles in the regulation of cytoskeletal organization and signal transduction, usually serving as molecular scaffolds that link signaling molecules to the cytoskeleton. Further analysis revealed that the expression of PDLIM5 in TECs was notably higher than that of other PDLIM family proteins (Supplementary Fig. 1b). PDLIM5, in particular, has been implicated in various cellular processes, including actin dynamics, cell adhesion and migration, and signal transduction14. Previous study found that high PDLIM5 expression in non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC) cells promoted cell migration and accelerated lung cancer metastasis by regulating epithelial-mesenchymal transition (EMT)15, suggesting that PDLIM5 is an important oncogenic gene. To gain a more comprehensive understanding of PDLIM5 expression in stromal cells within the tumor microenvironment, We compared PDLIM5 levels in stromal cells from tumors versus normal tissues. Beyond tumor cells, PDLIM5 expression was higher in TECs than in normal endothelial cells NECs (Fig. 1b). Similar results were observed in TECs isolated from mammary tumor models and human COLO205 subcutaneous graft tumors (Supplementary Fig. 1c–f).

To further analyze which subtypes of TECs highly expressed PDLIM5, we collected paired cancerous and adjacent normal tissues from seven patients with lung cancer. TECs are subdivided into five subtypes based on their unique gene transcription signatures: Arterial ECs (AECs), which are responsible for the transport of oxygenated blood away from the heart; Venous ECs (VECs), involved in returning deoxygenated blood to the heart; Lymphatic ECs (LECs), which play a role in immune surveillance and fluid balance; Capillary ECs (CapECs), which facilitate the exchange of nutrients, waste, and gases between blood and tissues; and TipECs, which are involved in angiogenesis, guiding the formation of new blood vessels (Fig. 1c, Supplementary Fig. 2a–e). Our results showed that, compared with those in NECs, the proportion of TipECs in TECs increased, whereas the proportion of CapECs and AECs decreased (Fig. 1d), which was consistent with previous studies5. This shift in cell subtype proportions reflected angiogenic phenotype during tumorigenesis. Further analysis revealed that PDLIM5 was upregulated in AECs, CapECs, LECs, and TipECs (Fig. 1e, Supplementary Fig. 2f). Consistent with our data, we re-analyzed the scRNA-seq dataset E-MTAB-6308 using their published methodology5, and PDLIM5 was significantly upregulated in TECs versus NECs across multiple activated subpopulations, including tip cells, artery ECs, immature ECs, and activated postcapillary vein ECs (Supplementary Fig. 2g). Additionally, in clinical lung cancer tissues, we observed higher expression of PDLIM5 in TECs compared to adjacent normal tissue ECs. Elevated PDLIM5 expression in ECs was correlated with poorer survival outcomes (Fig. 1f–h). Beyond lung cancer, patients with high PDLIM5 expression across several other cancer types also exhibited worse survival outcomes (Supplementary Fig. 3). This suggests that PDLIM5 in TECs might play a broader role in cancer progression.

A previous study showed that patients with NSCLC expressing high angiogenic TEC gene set signatures had shorter overall survival5. We hypothesized that the highly expressed cytoskeleton-associated protein PDLIM5 in TECs causes abnormal tip cell function and promotes angiogenesis. To test this hypothesis, we constructed a Lewis lung carcinoma (LLC) subcutaneous graft tumor model in Pdlim5 global-overexpressing (CAG-Pdlim5) mice. Results showed that tumors in CAG-Pdlim5 mice exhibited more rapid growth and more abundant vessels (Fig. 1i–m). These findings suggest that PDLIM5 promotes tumor angiogenesis in TECs.

Endothelial Pdlim5 deletion impedes tumor growth and angiogenesis
To further investigate the effect of endothelial PDLIM5 on tumor angiogenesis, we engineered a conditional knockout mouse model. We crossed Pdlim5flox/flox mice with Cdh5-CreERT2 mice to generate Pdlim5flox/flox; Cdh5 CreERT2 mice (Pdlim5cKO), allowing for specific deletion of Pdlim5 in ECs upon tamoxifen treatment (Supplementary Fig. 4a, b). This strategy allowed us to systematically evaluate the endothelial-specific role of PDLIM5 in tumor angiogenesis while maintaining its physiological function in other cell types. Notably, genetic ablation of endothelial Pdlim5 did not perturb normal tissue homeostasis or vascular integrity, as demonstrated by unaltered vascular density, and preserved endothelial permeability in Pdlim5cKO mice (Supplementary Fig. 4c, d). These findings were consistent with our previously published observations16.

To assess the role of PDLIM5 in tumor growth and angiogenesis, we employed three different subcutaneous xenograft tumor models using LLC lung cancer cells, Hepa1-6 hepatocellular carcinoma cells, and MC38 intestinal cancer cells (Fig. 2a, e, i). Across all three models, the deletion of Pdlim5 in ECs significantly attenuated tumor growth (Fig. 2b, c, f, g, j, k), concurrently reducing the density of CD31-positive vessels, indicating inhibited angiogenesis (Fig. 2d, h, l). These consistent findings across different tumor types suggest that PDLIM5 plays a crucial role in promoting angiogenesis in diverse tumor microenvironments. To extend these observations to an orthotopic setting, we constructed a breast cancer model using murine mammary E0771 cancer cells. Pdlim5 deletion in ECs inhibited orthotopic tumor growth and angiogenesis (Fig. 2m–p), reinforcing the broad relevance of PDLIM5 in tumor vascularization. To further validate PDLIM5 as a potential anti-angiogenic therapeutic target, we administered tamoxifen to induce endothelial Pdlim5 knockout in mice when tumor volume reached 60 mm3. The results demonstrated that both early and late Pdlim5 ablation significantly reduced tumor growth and neovascular density compared to the control group (Fig. 2q–u). This comprehensive approach, encompassing both subcutaneous and orthotopic models, highlights the universal role of PDLIM5 in facilitating tumor growth through angiogenesis.

PDLIM5 promotes filopodia formation and vessel sprouting
PDLIM5 is highly expressed in tip ECs, which are crucial for angiogenesis, and deletion of PDLIM5 inhibits tumor angiogenesis. It is difficult to directly observe the subtle morphological and functional changes of tip cells by immunofluorescence in tumour sections. To better elucidate PDLIM5’s role in tip cell function, we performed whole-mount staining of postnatal day 7 (P7) retinas, which allows for the visualization of tip cells and filopodia formation. Pdlim5 knockout significantly delayed the expansion of the retinal vascular plexus to the periphery (Fig. 3a), indicating its crucial role in angiogenesis. Further analysis revealed that vessel coverage, branching points, and the number of tip cells and filopodia were markedly reduced (Fig. 3b–e), highlighting PDLIM5’s involvement in vascular sprouting and expansion. However, retinal vascular networks in Pdlim5 knockout mice at P14 and P17 showed no significant defects compared with the control group (Supplementary Fig. 4e, f). These results suggest that PDLIM5 deficiency does not affect the final maturation and function of retinal vessels. Second, we utilized the aortic ring assay, a method that mimics vessel sprouting in Matrigel, allowing the assessment of sprouting angiogenesis in vitro. ECs with Pdlim5 deletion displayed defects in this assay (Fig. 3f–i), reinforcing the findings from the retinal model and emphasizing PDLIM5’s role in EC behavior. Lastly, to examine tip cell filopodia formation in vitro, we employed an EC fibrin bead assay (FBA), which provides a simplified and controlled setting to observe cellular behavior. Silencing PDLIM5 in ECs with two lentiviral vectors encoding different small hairpin RNA (shRNA) of PDLIM5 (shPDLIM5) effectively reduced PDLIM5 protein levels (Supplementary Fig. 5a). This knockdown (KD) led to a significant decrease in the sprouting area, number of tip cells, and filopodia (Fig. 3j–m, Supplementary Fig. 5b), further confirming the importance of PDLIM5 in tip cell function.

In addition, TECs isolated from Pdlim5 KO mice exhibited marked down-regulation of tip cell marker genes, including CXCR4, ESM1, and DLL4, when compared with those from control tumor-bearing mice (Supplementary Fig. 5c). Conversely, TECs from Pdlim5-overexpressing mice displayed an augmented sprouting area, accompanied by a larger quantity of tip cells and filopodia, in comparison to TECs from control tumor-bearing mice (Supplementary Fig. 5d, e). Taken together, these results imply that PDLIM5 facilitates tip cell filopodia formation and vessel sprouting.

To further investigate the role of endothelial PDLIM5 in angiogenesis, we first used a tube formation assay and found that PDLIM5 KD decreased tube length (Supplementary Fig. 5f, g). Conversely, PDLIM5 overexpression using a lentiviral vector encoding PDLIM5 increased tube length (Supplementary Fig. 5h–j). We also performed RNA-seq to assess the transcriptional landscape of control and PDLIM5 KD human umbilical vein ECs (HUVECs). Gene Ontology pathway analysis of differentially expressed genes (DEGs) revealed enrichment in angiogenesis, ECM organization, cell adhesion, and response to hypoxia pathways (Supplementary Fig. 5k). Genes enriched in these pathways were downregulated in PDLIM5 KD HUVECs, including collagen type IV alpha 1 (COL4A1), collagen type IV alpha 2 (COL4A2), matrix metalloproteinase-2 (MMP2), and vasohibin-1 (VASH1) (Supplementary Fig. 5l). RT-PCR further validated the downregulation of these genes in PDLIM5 KD HUVECs (Supplementary Fig. 5m). Previous studies have reported that these cell migration-related genes are regulated by integrin/focal adhesion kinase (FAK) signaling17, and our results showed that the FAK inhibitor Y15 suppressed the expression of VASH1, VEGFR3, and MMP2 (Supplementary Fig. 5n). We then investigated whether decreased filopodia formation in PDLIM5 KD HUVECs would also inhibit integrin/FAK signaling activation by reducing the response to the ECM. We found that PDLIM5 KD inhibited FAK activation, whereas PDLIM5 overexpression promoted FAK activation (Supplementary Fig. 5o). These results indicate that PDLIM5 deletion impedes FAK activation and filopodia formation in tip cells.

PDLIM5 promotes F-actin bundling during filopodia formation by interacting with ACTN1/ACTN4
To unravel the molecular mechanisms behind the defects in endothelial filopodia formation in the absence of PDLIM5, we hypothesized that PDLIM5 plays a crucial role through interactions with cytoskeletal proteins. To test this, we overexpressed PDLIM5 with a Flag tag in HUVECs, followed by Flag immunoprecipitation (IP) and mass spectrometry (MS) analysis (Fig. 4a, b), which led to the identification of 145 PDLIM5-interacting proteins, including actin. To further validate PDLIM5’s involvement in cell migration and adhesion, we analyzed adhesion datasets and found PDLIM5 at one of the highest frequencies among cell migration-related genes (Supplementary Fig. 6a), with 13 of these proteins also identified in the actin-binding gene set and meta-adhesome dataset. Our MS analysis specifically revealed that PDLIM5 interacts with actinin-1 (ACTN1) and actinin-4 (ACTN4), proteins critical for F-actin bundling and filopodia formation18,19. These interactions were confirmed by immunoblot analysis in both HEK293T cells and HUVECs (Fig. 4c, d), where PDLIM5 showed high co-localization with ACTN1/ACTN4 in the filopodia of tip cells (Fig. 4e, f, Supplementary Fig. 6b, c). To further validate the regulatory role of ACTN1/ACTN4 in FAK signaling and filopodia formation, we employed siRNA-mediated knockdown of ACTN1/ACTN4 in endothelial cells. Results showed that knocking down either ACTN1 or ACTN4 effectively suppressed FAK activation and tip cell filopodia formation (Supplementary Fig. 7a–e).

Moreover, PDLIM5 overexpression increased the binding of actin to ACTN1/ACTN4, whereas its deletion had the opposite effect (Fig. 4g). Additionally, overexpression of ACTN1 and ACTN4 promoted FAK and its downstream signaling pathways (Fig. 4h–l), whereas PDLIM5 KD abolished FAK activation and the expression of DLL4, VASH1, and MMP2, highlighting PDLIM5’s pivotal role in regulating these pathways essential for filopodia formation and angiogenesis. In conclusion, our results demonstrate that PDLIM5 interacts with ACTN1/ACTN4 to regulate filopodia formation and angiogenesis through cytoskeletal dynamics and FAK signaling.

LIMs domain S593/F596 is critical for the interaction of PDLIM5 with ACTN1/ACTN4
PDLIM5, in addition to being a cytoskeleton-binding protein, functions as a scaffolding protein because of its unique structural domains: a PDZ domain at its N-terminus and three LIM domains at its C-terminus. To understand how PDLIM5 interacts with actin and its binding partners, ACTN1/ACTN4, we conducted a series of experiments to delineate the specific binding sites. We found that PDLIM5 binds to ACTN1/ACTN4 via its LIM domains (Fig. 5a, Supplementary Fig. 8a, b) and binds to actin through its PDZ domain (Supplementary Fig. 8c). This dual interaction suggests that PDLIM5 acts as a scaffolding protein, facilitating the binding of ACTN1/ACTN4 to actin.

To further elucidate the molecular mechanism, we performed molecular docking analysis, which revealed multiple binding sites between the LIM domains of PDLIM5 to the ACTN1/ACTN4 (Supplementary Fig. 8d, e). Sequence comparisons identified conserved sites (R240, S354, K582, S593, and F596) in PDLIM5, which were predicted to interact with both ACTN1 and ACTN4 (Fig. 5b, Supplementary Fig. 8f, g). Mutational analysis of these sites revealed that the S593A and F596L mutations significantly reduced the binding of PDLIM5 to ACTN1/ACTN4, but not F-actin (Fig. 5c, d, Supplementary Fig. 8h), with molecular docking confirming the high similarity in binding regions (Fig. 5e, f). To further validate these findings, we constructed a double-mutant PDLIM5 (S593A/F596L), which further attenuated the binding of PDLIM5 to ACTN1/ACTN4 (Fig. 5g). The binding of the mutated LIM domain to ACTN1/ACTN4 was also weakened (Supplementary Fig. 8i), demonstrating the critical role of these sites in the interaction.

Filopodia formation, which relies on the bundling of actin filaments, is regulated by the interaction of ACTN1/ACTN4 with actin. We found that this regulatory mechanism can be disrupted by specific mutations in PDLIM5, as evidenced by the significantly attenuated binding of ACTN1/ACTN4 to actin after the S593A and F596L mutations (Fig. 5h, i). These results indicate that PDLIM5 interacts with ACTN1/ACTN4 through the S593/F596 residues, and acts as a scaffolding protein by promoting F-actin binding to ACTN1/ACTN4 (Fig. 5j). The above results demonstrate that PDLIM5 plays a pivotal role in filopodia formation through its interaction with cytoskeletal proteins.

S593A/F596L is indispensable for PDLIM5-induced tip cell filopodia formation and tumor angiogenesis
To determine whether the S593/F596-mediated interaction with ACTN1/ACTN4 contributes to the biological function of PDLIM5, we first evaluated the effect of the S593A/F596L mutation on tip cell filopodia formation. Results showed that re-expression of wild-type (WT) PDLIM5, but not the S593A/F596L-mutated PDLIM5, increased the number of tip cells and filopodia in PDLIM5 KD ECs (Fig. 6a–d). Additionally, tube length was also inhibited in PDLIM5 mutated HUVECs (Supplementary Fig. 9a, b). To validate these results in vivo, we used an adeno-associated virus (AAV) carrying a Tie2 promoter to overexpress WT and S588A/F591L (mouse homolog of human PDLIM5 S593/F596)-mutated Pdlim5 in TECs by multi-point injection into the tumor (Fig. 6e). The results showed that Pdlim5 was successfully overexpressed in the tumor vessels (Supplementary Fig. 9c). WT Pdlim5 significantly enhanced tumor growth and angiogenesis compared with Pdlim5cKO mice, whereas the mutated Pdlim5 group showed no such effect, exhibiting tumor growth rates (Fig. 6f–h) and angiogenesis levels (Fig. 6i, j) comparable to those observed in the Pdlim5cKO group. Thus, the interaction of PDLIM5 with ACTN1/ACTN4 through S593/F596 is critical for promoting tumor angiogenesis and growth, as evidenced by the lack of these effects when these sites are mutated.

Deletion of endothelial Pdlim5 promotes tumor vascular normalization and T cell infiltration
The tumor microenvironment typically induces morphological and functional defects in the tumor vasculature, resulting in increased hypoxia, suppressed immune cell function, and impaired delivery of chemotherapeutic agents due to low perfusion levels and high permeability20,21. To address these issues, we investigated the effect of PDLIM5 deficiency on tumor hypoxia and vascular function. Our findings reveal that Pdlim5 deletion in TECs ameliorated intratumoral hypoxia (Fig. 7a, Supplementary Fig. 10a–d), suggesting an improvement in oxygenation within the tumor. Concurrently, Pdlim5 knockout led to increased coverage of smooth muscle actin (SMA)-positive pericytes around blood vessels (Fig. 7b, Supplementary Fig. 10e–g), which is indicative of enhanced vascular stability and maturation. Tumor vessel perfusion was also improved in Pdlim5-deficient mice, as assessed by fluorescein isothiocyanate (FITC)-lectin staining (Fig. 7b), implying better blood flow. Furthermore, we observed a reduction in tumor hemorrhage with decreased presence of Ter119-positive blood cells in the interstitial space (Supplementary Fig. 10h–k) and a decrease in tumor vessel permeability (Supplementary Fig. 10l–o). These combined effects indicate that the loss of Pdlim5 in TECs not only alleviates hypoxia but also promotes the normalization of the tumor vasculature, potentially enhancing immune cell function, thereby providing a therapeutic advantage in chemosensitization and immunotherapy.

Previous studies have shown that normalization of tumor vessels can inhibit tumor metastasis22–24. Therefore, to determine the effects of Pdlim5 knockout on tumor metastasis, we established subcutaneous LLC tumor xenografts, performed surgical resection of the primary tumors, and analyzed lung metastasis after tumor regrowth. Results showed that Pdlim5 deletion significantly inhibited LLC cell lung metastasis (Supplementary Fig. 11a–c). Further, we analyzed whether Pdlim5 knockout-induced tumor vessel normalization could enhance the efficacy of low-dose chemotherapy. Results showed that low-dose cisplatin (4 mg/kg) combined with Pdlim5 deletion further reduced tumor growth and compared to cisplatin alone (Supplementary Fig. 11d–j).

Normalized tumor vessels enhance T cell infiltration and anti-tumor immunity through structural and functional remodeling3,25–29. Therefore, we aimed to further investigate whether tumor vascular normalization induced by Pdlim5 deletion can promote T cell infiltration. We first examined the proportions of CD4+ and CD8+ T cells in tumors by using multicolor immunofluorescence (Supplementary Fig. 12a) and flow cytometry (Supplementary Fig. 13a, b). The proportions of both CD4+ and CD8+ T cells were increased in the endothelial Pdlim5 deletion group (Fig. 7c, Supplementary Fig. 12a). A leukocyte trans-endothelial migration assay was conducted to evaluate the efficiency of T-cell trans-endothelial migration, which revealed that genetic ablation of Pdlim5 significantly promoted this migratory process (Fig. 7d).

The accumulation of ICAM1 on the EC membrane facilitates T cell adhesion and transendothelial transport30–32, and flow cytometry analysis confirmed increased membrane aggregation of ICAM1 in PDLIM5-knockdown HUVECs (Fig. 7e, Supplementary Fig. 13c). This suggests that the mechanism underlying the increased T cell infiltration induced by PDLIM5 deletion includes not only vascular structural and functional normalization, but also enhanced T cell adhesion in tumor vessels through upregulation of ICAM1. But how does PDLIM5 loss promote ICAM1 membrane accumulation? Previous studies have shown that endothelial ICAM1 binds to ACTN1/ACTN4 to stabilize its membrane aggregation and enhance T-cell adhesion33,34. And our molecular docking results predicted that PDLIM5 also interacts with ACTN1/ACTN4 (Fig. 5e, f), suggesting that PDLIM5 and ICAM1 competitively bind to ACTN1 and ACTN4. Further validation revealed that PDLIM5 knockdown increased the binding of ICAM1 to ACTN4 (Fig. 7f). Atomic force microscopy (AFM) detection also showed that PDLIM5 deficiency reduced endothelial cell stiffness (Fig. 7g). Collectively, these findings demonstrate that PDLIM5 deficiency promotes structural and functional normalization of tumor vessels, increases the accumulation of ICAM1 on the endothelial cell membrane and reduces endothelial cell stiffness, thereby promoting T cell adhesion and transendothelial migration, and enhancing T cell infiltration into tumors.

Deletion of endothelial Pdlim5 improves immunotherapy response by increasing T-cell infiltration
To further elucidate the potential sensitizing effect of endothelial Pdlim5 deletion on immunotherapy, we administered an anti-PD-L1 monoclonal antibody (10 mg/kg) every three days when tumors reached 60 mm3 in tumor-bearing mice (Fig. 8a). Mice treated with the anti-PD-L1 monoclonal antibody exhibited minimal inhibitory effects on LLC tumor growth (Fig. 8b–d), consistent with previous reports indicating that LLC tumors are insensitive to anti-PD-1/PD-L1 immunotherapy35,36. However, in striking contrast, Pdlim5-knockout mice treated with the anti-PD-L1 monoclonal antibody showed a significant reduction in tumor size. This reduction in tumor growth was accompanied by a substantial increase in the infiltration of CD4+ and CD8+ T cells (Fig. 8b–h), highlighting the enhanced immune response facilitated by PDLIM5 deletion.

These results demonstrate that PDLIM5 deletion not only ameliorates the tumor vascular abnormalities but also significantly enhances the antitumor efficacy of the anti-PD-L1 monoclonal antibody. Our findings indicate that PDLIM5 deletion promotes tumor susceptibility to immunotherapy, as evidenced by the smaller tumor sizes and increased T-cell infiltration in Pdlim5-knockout mice receiving PD-L1 monoclonal antibody treatment, providing compelling evidence for targeting tumor vasculature to improve immune responses and immunotherapy outcomes (Fig. 8i).

## Methods

Cell culture
Normal lung ECs and tumor ECs were isolated from mouse lung tissues and tumor tissues as previously described in ref. 5. Briefly, freshly dissected tissues were minced into small fragments and enzymatically digested using collagenase type I (1 mg/mL; Sigma-Aldrich, C0130) and DNase I (30 µg/mL; Sigma-Aldrich, DN25) at 37 °C for 45 minutes with gentle agitation. The resulting single-cell suspensions were filtered through 70 µm cell strainers and subjected to magnetic-activated cell sorting (MACS) using anti-CD31 microbeads (Miltenyi Biotec, 130-097-418) to enrich endothelial cells. The purified cells were cultured in Endothelial Cell Growth Medium-2 (EGM-2; Lonza, CC-3162) supplemented with 10% fetal bovine serum (FBS). HUVECs were obtained from the Cell Bank of the Chinese Academy of Sciences (Shanghai, China) and maintained in EGM-2 medium. HEK 293T (CRL-3216, ATCC), LLC (CRL-1642, ATCC), Hepa1-6 (CRL-1830, ATCC), MC38 (ENH204-EP, NCI/NIH), and E0771 (CRL-3461, ATCC) cells were cultured in Dulbecco’s modified Eagle’s medium (KGL1211-500, KeyGEN) supplemented with 10% FBS (F101-01, Vazyme). All cells were cultured at 37 °C and 5% CO2.

Mice
Sex was not considered as a biological variable. Both male and female mice were used in this study. Pdlim5f/f mice were generously provided by Ju Chen (Department of Medicine and Cardiology, University of California San Diego, La Jolla (CA)). Details of Pdlim5f/f mice have been described previously16. Cdh5-CreERT2 mice were purchased from GemPharmatech Co., Ltd. (Nanjing, China; strain no. T052686). Pdlim5f/f mice were mated with Cdh5-cre Ert2 mice to generate the Pdlim5f/f: Cdh5-creErt2 genotype. To induce Pdlim5 deletion in ECs, mice received intraperitoneal injections of 100 µL tamoxifen (25 mg/mL) daily for five consecutive days. CAG-Pdlim5-polyATG mice were purchased from GemPharmatech (Jiangsu, China). For all in vivo experiments, 8–10-week-old mice of both sexes were used unless otherwise specified. Mice were housed under specific pathogen-free (SPF) conditions with controlled temperature (22±2 °C), humidity (50±10%), and a 12-hour light/dark cycle, with free access to food and water. All procedures were approved by the Animal Care and Use Committee of Zhejiang University School of Medicine (ZJU20220531). The mice were maintained in the specific pathogen-free facility of the Laboratory of Animal Research at the International School of Medicine, Zhejiang University.

Proteomics analysis
HUVECs were transduced with a lentiviral vector encoding PDLIM5 with a C-terminal Flag tag for 48 h, subsequently lysed in IP buffer (50 mM Tris-HCl (pH 7.5), 150 mM NaCl, 1% NP-40, 0.5% sodium deoxycholate, 0.1% sodium dodecyl sulfate, 1 mM ethylenediaminetetraacetic acid, and protease inhibitors) and incubated with magnetic anti-FLAG beads overnight at 4 °C. After washing, proteins were eluted, concentrated, and subjected to in-gel digestion. Gel bands or spots were cut into approximately 1 mm³ pieces, destained, dehydrated, and reduced with 10 mM dithiothreitol at 37 °C for 1 hour, followed by alkylation with 55 mM iodoacetamide in the dark for 30 minutes. After dehydration, gel pieces were washed with deionized water, rehydrated in 50 mM ammonium bicarbonate, and digested with trypsin overnight at 37 °C. Peptides were extracted, combined, and desalted using C18 columns. Liquid chromatography–tandem mass spectrometry was performed with a Q Exactive HF-X mass spectrometer (Thermo Fisher Scientific Inc) using Nanospray Flex™ ion source with a 1 µg sample. The liquid chromatography conditions included a flow rate of 600 nL/min and a gradient from 8% to 95% acetonitrile over 60 minutes. Protein identification was performed using the human database with Proteome Discoverer 2.4 software. The protein mass spectrometry sequencing data were uploaded to the iProX database (https://www.iprox.cn/page/home.html). The Project ID is IPX0010745000, and the ProteomeXchange ID is PXD059449.

RNA-sequencing analysis
Total RNA was isolated from HUVECs transfected with shPDLIM5 or shScr lentivirus for 48 h using an RNA-Quick Purification Kit (ES-RN001, Yishan Biotechnology). Subsequently, cDNA libraries were constructed and sequenced by the Beijing Genomics Institute using the BGISEQ-500 platform. The bioinformatics workflow was performed according to procedures established by Dr. TOM (BGI). A false discovery rate-corrected p-value of 0.05 was considered statistically significant. The corresponding raw data were uploaded to the Genome Sequence Archive (GSA) (Project No.: HRA009823).

In vivo xenograft assays
In subcutaneous xenograft tumor models, LLC cells, Hepa1-6 cells, and MC38 cells (2×106 cells suspended in 100 µl phosphate-buffered saline (PBS)) were injected subcutaneously into the right flank. Tumor volumes were measured every two days and calculated using the formula: length × width²/2 and was measured with a digital caliper. For orthotopic breast tumor growth, 2×106 E0771 cells were orthotopically injected into the mammary fat pads of mice. In accordance with Institutional Animal Care and Use Committee (IACUC)-approved protocols at the Fourth Affiliated Hospital, Zhejiang University School of Medicine, the maximum permitted tumor burden was defined as a longest tumor diameter of ≤2.0 cm (approximately ≤ 1500–2000 mm³). Mice were euthanized at or before this threshold, or earlier if humane endpoints were reached, including tumor ulceration or necrosis, impaired mobility or feeding, severe distress, or body-weight loss exceeding 15%.
For in vivo rescue experiments, when the tumor grew to ~60 mm3, 50 µl AAV-Pdlim5 wild type (WT) or AAV-Pdlim5 mutation (MUT) adeno-associated virus (AAV) with a titer of 1×108 viral particles/µL was injected at multiple points within the tumors for twice. Pdlim5f/f and Pdlim5f/f: Cdh5-creErt2 mice were divided into four groups (n=5 per group): Pdlim5f/f or Pdlim5f/f: Cdh5-creErt2 mice injected with AAV-vector, Pdlim5f/f: Cdh5-creErt2 mice injected with AAV-Pdlim5 WT, and Pdlim5f/f: Cdh5-creErt2 mice injected with AAV-Pdlim5 MUT. The mice were euthanized by CO2 asphyxia when the experiments concluded or when the longest dimension of the tumors no more than 2.0 cm. The excised tumors were weighed and then either fixed with 4% paraformaldehyde (PFA) or stored at −80 °C until further analysis.
To elucidate the effect of PDLIM5 deletion on tumor vessel perfusion and leakage, we conducted assays for hypoxia in the tumor microenvironment, pimonidazole staining, and vascular leakage and perfusion, as previously described. Tumor hypoxia was quantified with a Hypoxyprobe kit (HP1-100, Hypoxyprobe) in accordance with the manufacturer’s instructions. To evaluate vascular permeability, 100 µl of FITC-conjugated dextran (25 µg/mL, 70 kDa, FD70, Sigma-Aldrich) was administered intravenously to the mice, followed by perfusion with 1% PFA solution 30 min later. Subsequently, the tumors were dissected and embedded in Tissue-Tek OCT compound for subsequent analysis. To quantify vessel perfusion, we administered intravenous injections of DyLight 488-conjugated Tomato lectin (1 mg/mL, 100 µL, DL-1174-1, Vector Laboratories) 30 min before sacrificing the mice, after which the tumors were harvested.
To explore the synergistic effect of PDLIM5 deletion on cisplatin treatment, tumor-bearing mice were intraperitoneally injected with 4 mg/kg cisplatin (MCE, HY-17394) dissolved in saline every 3 days starting at tumor volume ≈60 mm3; control groups received equal-volume saline injections (n=5/group), with tumor dimensions monitored by caliper every 2 days (volume=0.5×L×W²).
In experiments utilizing immunotherapeutic checkpoint inhibitors, 200 µg (10 mg/kg) of anti-PD-L1 monoclonal antibody (BioXcell, BE0101) or isotype immunoglobulin G was administered intraperitoneally to each mouse at 3-day intervals. Mice were subsequently sacrificed at the indicated times, and tumors were collected for subsequent analysis.

Patients and samples
All human studies complied with institutional and national ethical regulations and were approved by the Medical Ethics Committee of the Fourth Affiliated Hospital, Zhejiang University School of Medicine (Approval No.: K2022179). Written informed consent was obtained from all participants prior to sample collection. For single-cell RNA sequencing, paired tumor and adjacent non-tumor lung tissues were prospectively collected from seven patients with NSCLC between November 2022 and January 2023 at the Fourth Affiliated Hospital of Zhejiang University (Yiwu, Zhejiang, China). Fresh specimens were enzymatically dissociated immediately after surgical resection to obtain single-cell suspensions for library construction and sequencing.
For immunofluorescence (IF) analysis, paired tumor and adjacent non-tumor tissues from an additional ten patients were used to compare PDLIM5 expression levels in endothelial cells (CD31+). PDLIM5 fluorescence intensity was quantified using ImageJ software and normalized to DAPI to control for cell density. For survival analysis, paraffin-embedded tumor samples from twenty NSCLC patients were subjected to IF staining for PDLIM5 and CD31 to stratify cases into PDLIM5-high and PDLIM5-low endothelial expression groups based on median signal intensity. Overall survival (OS) was calculated from diagnosis to death or last follow-up. Survival curves were analyzed by Kaplan–Meier log-rank test and multivariate Cox proportional hazards regression using GraphPad Prism (v8.0.1), with statistical significance defined as p<0.05. Comprehensive clinicopathological information of all patients is provided in Supplementary Table 6.

Single-cells sequencing and data analysis
The lung tissues were dissociated into single-cell suspensions to facilitate further analysis. Single-cell suspensions were prepared at a concentration of 1×105 cells/mL in PBS and loaded onto microfluidic devices. scRNA-seq libraries were constructed using the GEXSCOPE® Single-Cell RNA Library Kit (Singleron Biotechnologies, China). Next, the individual libraries were diluted to 4 ng/µL and subsequently pooled for sequencing. The pooled libraries were subjected to sequencing on an Illumina NovaSeq 6000 instrument with 150 bp paired-end reads. Additionally, the raw data were subjected to a series of processing steps to generate the gene expression profiles. This was achieved using CeleScope v1.14.0, a software package developed by Singleron Biotechnologies, with the default parameters retained. The Scanpy package, version 1.8.1, was utilized for quality control, dimensionality reduction, and cluster analysis in the Python 3.7 programming language. We filtered the expression matrix by the following criteria: 1) cells with gene count less than 200 or with top 2% gene count were excluded; 2) cells with the top 2% UMI count were excluded; 3) cells with mitochondrial content >20% were excluded; 4) genes expressed in less than 5 cells were excluded. The batch effect was removed using the Harmony software. Furthermore, the DEGs were identified by comparing the two groups using the Wilcoxon rank-sum test with the standard parameters applied. Genes were considered differentially expressed if they were expressed in at least 10% of the cells in either of the two groups and exhibited an adjusted p-value below a threshold of 0.05. This was calculated through the Benjamini-Hochberg correction for multiple hypothesis testing. The human single-cell transcriptomics data are deposited under the accessions: HRA012795.

Statistical analysis
The presented data are derived from a minimum of three biologically independent experiments and analyzed using GraphPad Prism 8.0 software (GraphPad Software, La Jolla, CA). Statistical significance between individual groups was evaluated using two-tailed independent Student’s t-tests. When examining multiple groups, a one-way or two-way analysis of variance was performed. Survival differences were assessed using the Kaplan-Meier method, and statistical significance was determined using the log-rank test. Statistical significance was set at p-value <0.05, and this is indicated in the figures as follows: p<0.05 (*), p<0.01 (**), p<0.001 (***), with “ns” denoting “not significant,” as indicated in the figure legends.

### Reviewer 1

In this study, the authors investigate the role of PDLIM5 in the tumor microenvironment, focusing on its effects on tip cells and vascular normalization, immune cell infiltration, and response to anti-PD-L1 immunotherapy. Using a combination of integrative gene expression analysis, single-cell RNA sequencing, and functional experiments, they demonstrate that PDLIM5 expression is increased in tumor endothelial cells, associated with tumor neuovascularization, and functionally validated using in vitro cell assay and in vivo tumor modeling that PDLIM5 is linked to tumor vascularization, reduces tumor hypoxia, and enhances T cell infiltration, thereby improving the efficacy of immune checkpoint therapy. Using molecular docking and co-IP, the study reported that PDLIM5 interact with the ACTIN2/4, hencing regulating filopodia formation and angiogenesis. The study spans multiple tumor models, including Hepa1-6, MC38, and LLC, to validate these findings. The study has applied a comprehensive molecular and cellular approaches to evaluate the effect of PDLIM5 on tumor vasuclar functions, the molecular interactions with ACTIN2/4, and its implications for cancer therapy.
While the manuscript employs a variety of experimental approaches, the work is also hindered by several limitations, including the conclusion on Tip endothelial cells, the molecular mechanisms linking PDLIM5 to normal vascular functions in tissues and tumor neovascularization, the prognostic value of PDLIM5 expression and patient outcome, as well as critical components of the immune microenvironment. Furthermore, there are quite a number of mistakes in the figures and supplementary figures, which will need significant proof reading and checking the original results. Detial comments for these concerns are highlighted below. Carefully addressing these are required before any possible consideration of the study for publication.
1. One major conclusion of this study is the PDLIM5 affects endothelial tip cell filopodia formation and tumor angiogenesis. Tip cells are a very small fraction of endothelial cells leading the vascular angiogenesis. While tip cells are almost absence in adult normal tissues, this endothelial phenotype is increased in tumors and essential for tumor neovascularization. Furthermore, tip cells are well characterized with the expression of classic markers such as CXCR4, ESM1, DLL4. The current study had used COL4A1, PLVAP, COL4A2 as markers for TipECs, which are not correct (Figure S2C). These are mixed markers for EndoMT EC phenotypes. These jeopardize the conclusiveness of the results and conclusion made based on Figure 1 and related figures.
For example, in TEC (Figure 1d), the fraction of tip ECs could not be over 20% of the entire ECs. Furthermore, the increase expression of PDLIM5 is not specific to TipECs. According to the data presented in Figure 1b, as well as checking the gene expression data provided by the protein atlas database, PDLIM5 is higher expressed in vascular smooth muscle cells, skeletal monocytes, fibroblasts. Similarly, the increased PDLIM5 was not restricted to TipECs, as noted by the authors in the manuscript (line 95-96). Thus, the annotation and interpretation of TipECs will require significant revision and correction.
2. Regarding the association between PDLIM5 expression and prognostic outcome of cancer patients (Figure 1h, and supplementary Figure 3), I am not completely sure if these data have been correctly adjusted and calculated. First, neither the main text or supplementary methods describe how these Kaplan-Meier curve have been generated, and the data source used to analysis the probability of overall survival with PDLIM5 expression. It is presumably coming from the TCGA database. However, when checking the survival data from the TCGA (https://tcga-survival.com/data-table?view=gene) or from the HPA, the expression of PDLIM5 did not show the same trajectory as what the figures provided in Supplementary Figure 3. The authors will have to clearly documented their analysis and scripts in the methods.
3. The selective effect of PDLIM5 on tumor vasculature formation. It is plausible that the study has used both in vitro, ex vivo and in vivo models to study the effect of PDLIM5 on tumor vasculature formation. First, it remains unclear how and why loss of PDLIM5 do not affect the development of normal tissue vasculature and functions (Supplementary Figure 4c-e) but exhibit clear effect on the tumor vasculatures with the ectopic PDX models. What is the phenotype of PDLIM5cKO mice if the induction of condition PDLIM5 was induced at birth or during fetal stages? In Figure 3, the study has already demonstrated that postnatal PDLIM5 knockout in ECs inhibit vessel sprouting in retina. This contradict with the conclusion made in part 1 (line 119-120).
It is unclear in the current methods provided, at what ages were the TAM induction was introduced. PDLIM5 is not EC- specifically expressed, when addressing and validating the conditional KO models, it is essential to showed in Figure 2, as in Figure 1f, that PDLIM5 is not expressed by CD31 positive endothelial cells. These difference between adult and neonatal could potentially be due to the induction time.
4. The authors have done a great work in conducting all these experiments. However, it is very important to present the results clearly and correctly. Here I highlighted a few major mistakes in the manuscript figures and results.
Figure 4 g-l, the IP results show that shPDLIM5 down regulates DLL4, MMP2, p-FAK Y397, and VASH1 (g-h). However, quantification of IP in Figure 4i-l, show that shPDLIM5 increase their levels. Which of these are correct?
Size of FAK and p-FAK Y397. The protein size of FAK appears to be 100kDa in some figures (S7) and 120kDa in the other (S5, S9, Figure 4). And VEGFR3 appears to be 120kDa in S7, and 180kDa in S5.
All these kinds of mistakes should be carefully checked, as well as the original source data.
5. Methods regarding PDLIM5 knockdown in HUVECs. It is unclear about the methodology used for ACTIN1, ACTIN4, and PDLIM5 knockdown in HUVECs. For ACTIN1 and ACTIN4, synthetic siRNAs should have been used according to the methods. However, PDLIM5, why shRNA expressed by lentiviral have been used instead? Any reason for choosing the difference delivery approach? Please also check the siRNA sequences for si-ACTN1-1#, as it could not be found in the human ACTN1 gene.
6. The study has integreated public scRNA-seq data and generated new data based on their own patient cohort, but the current analysis and detial provided is not sufficient to support the reproducibility. What quality control metrics and thresholds were applied to filter low-quality cells, number of cells, number of patients and metadata, how batch effects had been handled if any, how were endothelial cell subtypes identified, marker genes used. Providing these details would strengthen the accuracy and reproducibility of the scRNA-seq analysis. Additionally, consider depositing the raw data and scripts in a public repository to enhance transparency.
7. The methods provide useful details about AAV injections and xenograft experiments, but there are areas requiring clarification: Specify the AAV titer (viral particles/μL) used for intratumoral injections to ensure reproducibility. Provide details on time points for tumor volume measurements and angiogenesis assessments after AAV injection.
Specify the exact frequency of tumor volume measurements within this period (e.g., daily or every other day). Clarify whether tumor volume data were averaged across multiple tumors or cohorts. Discuss variations in tumor growth rates over time to better contextualize the presented data.
8. The authors suggest that PDLIM5 could be a promising therapeutic target and mention small molecule inhibitors as a potential strategy. However, there is no experimental data, such as preclinical trials or efficacy studies, to back up these claims. Including some preliminary studies that explore inhibitors targeting PDLIM5 or its interaction sites would help demonstrate whether this approach could actually be effective in a therapeutic setting.

### Reviewer 2
