### Reviewer 3

This paper investigates the role of the cytoskeletal scaffold protein PDLIM5 in promoting angiogenesis by tumor endothelial cells (TECs). The authors show that PDLIM5 stimulates vascular sprouting in the retina of healthy mice as well as in tumor grafts. By combining KO of PDLIM5 with anti-PD-L1 treatment, they further show that this PDLIM5 function can be exploited to decrease tumor growth and promote tumor immune cell infiltration, suggesting that small molecules directed against PDLIM5 might hold promise as a new antitumor treatment. To address the mechanism underlying this PDLIM5 function and identify potential PDLIM5 surfaces to target for drug development, the authors examine the interaction between PDLIM5 and ACTN1/ACTN4, which has previously been reported in other cell types. In contrast to Nakagawa et al (2006), they find that PDLIM5 binds to ACTN1/ACTN4 through its Lim domain instead of its PDZ domain. They further narrow the PDLIM5- ACTN1/4 interaction down to two residues in the third LIM domain (S593 and F596) and present some data that suggests this interaction enhances the binding of ACTN1/ACTN4 to F-actin, thereby stabilizing and promoting filopodia formation and angiogenesis. In line with this, expression of the PDLIM5 double mutant in PDLIM KO mice hampers tumor growth, angiogenesis and immune cell invasion. The merit of this work mainly lies in the large body of data supporting PDLIM5 as a potentially interesting antitumor target for a great many different types of cancer. However, the described underlying mechanism is not fully supported by the data presented. Thus, to substantiate the claim that this study identified a druggable surface on PDLIM5, the authors will have to address the issues raised below.
Fig. 4: The authors claim that PDLIM5 recruits ACTN1/4 to actin in filopodia, however the linescans from the images shown in Fig. 4e-f do not show that higher PDLIM5 signals correspond to higher ACTN1/4 signals. In addition, the immunoprecipitation assay in Fig. 4g, shows varying levels of PDLIM5 in WCL, but does not confirm that this also corresponds to varying levels of PDLIM5 bound to actin after IP. Hence, they cannot conclude that PDLIM5 regulates the amount of ACTN1/4 bound to actin. To claim that PDLIM5 recruits ACTN1/4 to F-actin, they need to show that the level of PDLIM5 bound to F-actin after immunoprecipitation changes similarly as the level of ACTN1/4 bound to F-actin after immunoprecipitation.
In addition Line 193: The authors state that PDLIM5 colocalizes with ACTN1/4 in tip cells (Fig. 4e). Are the cells that are shown in the images and that are used for the linescans actual tip cells?
Fig 5: The authors should explain why Fig. 5g shows that PDLIM5 mutants bind less ACTN1/4, however the reverse IP in Fig, 5c-d does not show the same result. Is this perhaps due to the fact that these IP experiments were performed with full length PDLIM5, which can bind to F-actin and ACTN1/4. ### Reviewer 4

In the study entitled “Endothelial PDLIM5 promotes tip cell filopodia formation and tumor angiogenesis by regulating ACTN1/ACTN4-dependent actin bundling”, the authors investigate the role of PDZ and LIM domain 5 (PDLIM5) in tumor endothelial cell (TEC)-mediated angiogenesis. They demonstrate that PDLIM5 is highly expressed in lung cancer TECs, correlates with poor patient survival, and plays a crucial role in filopodia formation by interacting with actinin-1/actinin-4 (ACTN1/ACTN4) to facilitate filamentous actin (F-actin) bundling. Endothelial-specific deletion of PDLIM5 disrupts sprouting angiogenesis, reduces tumor growth, normalizes tumor vasculature, and enhances immunotherapy response in resistant tumors. These findings suggest that PDLIM5 may serve as a novel therapeutic target to improve cancer treatment outcomes.
Comments:
The results presented in the manuscript provide substantial evidence on the role of PDLIM5 in TECs and its potential impact on tumor angiogenesis. However, a number of comments should be addressed to support the claims and findings presented in the manuscript. These include:
• Additional functional studies are needed to convincingly demonstrate that endothelial PDLIM5 regulates tip cell function. For instance, in vitro migration assays and competition sprouting assays, where a mixed population WT and PDLIM5-silenced cells compete for the tip cell position, could provide additional strenght.
It would be also important to investigate how the tip cell subset (as well as the additional subtypes) is affected in the endothelial-specific PDLIM5 KO in mice.
• While the authors propose that endothelial PDLIM5 deletion induces tumor vessel normalization (TVN), Figure 2 suggests vessel pruning (reduced vessel density), which is likely responsible for the observed reduced tumor growth. This discrepancy warrants an explanation. TVN is often associated with improved metastasis outcomes rather than with an effect on primary tumor growth. It would be useful to investigate the relationship between vessel pruning and reduced tumor growth and explore whether TVN by PDLIM5 deletion affects metastasis.
• The mechanism by which endothelial PDLIM5 regulates T cell infiltration needs further investigations. Are increased T cell infiltration levels due to enhanced delivery upon TVN, or is there an effect on adhesion molecules? ICAM-1 clustering and function has been shown to be directly linked to ACTN4 (Celli et al. J Immunol. 2006). Thus, it would be crucial to assess whether PDLIM5 deletion alters ICAM-1 clustering. Additionally, as actin-binding proteins can differentially regulate EC stiffness (Schaefer, et al. J Cell 2014), it would be valuable to investigate whether PDLIM5 deletion leads to changes in EC stiffness that might favor T cell transmigration.
• ACTN4 is known to bind endothelial eNOS and inhibit its basal activity (Hiroi Yet al. FASEB J. 2008). Furthermore, as previoulsy shown by the authors, PDLIM5 phosphorylates eNOS to regulate NO generation, which can affect vessel permeability. It would be insightful to assess whether these mechanisms, particularly in relation to NO regulation and endothelial permeability, contribute to the in vivo phenotype observed upon PDLIM5 deletion. Could these factors also play a role in promoting T cell infiltration by modulating the permeability of tumor vessels?
• Given the evidence for improved perfusion in tumors with normalized vasculature, it would be useful to consider the potential effects of PDLIM5 deletion on chemotherapy efficacy. Better tumor perfusion could result in more effective drug delivery, independent of whether the treatment is chemotherapy or immunotherapy, unless the central mechanism is immune-mediated.
Minor:
In Figure 4I-M, the indication of sh vs. scr conditions appears to be swapped.

Response: (a) We sincerely appreciate the reviewer’s insightful questions and concerns. For the first
question, regarding the differential effects of PDLIM5 knockout (KO) on normal vascular development
versus tumor vasculature. Normal vascular development (e.g., retinal angiogenesis) is a tightly regulated,
programmed process with distinct phases of sprouting, maturation, and pruning. In the retina angiogenesis
experiments, Cdh5 Cre-mediated PDLIM5 deletion was induced in newborn mice by intraperitoneal (i.p.)
injections of 50 µl tamoxifen (1(cid:3031)mg/ml) from postnatal day 1 (P1) to P3. postnatal PDLIM5 KO in ECs
inhibited retinal vessel sprouting at P7 (Figure 3), which is consistent with its role in active angiogenesis.
In mice, the period from P1 to P7 marks the formation of the retinal vascular network. During this time,
angiogenesis proceeds continuously. Subsequently, from P7 to P14, the vascular maturation period
occurs. The vascular walls gradually reach maturity, with the connections between endothelial cells
tightening. After P14, the retinal blood vessels enter the remodeling stage. Here, the vessels are optimized
in accordance with the functional requirements of the retina. Unnecessary vascular branches are pruned,
rendering the vascular network more stable and efficient. We further examined the retinal vascular density
in PDLIM5 knockout mice on P14 and P17. The results indicated that PDLIM5 KO had no impact on the
vascular density of mice on these two time points (Response Fig 2A-D). We have now included Response

and was measured with a digital caliper. Tumor volume data were averaged across multiple tumors within
each experimental cohort. These variations in growth rates have been incorporated into the results section
of the manuscript, along with corresponding graphs that clearly illustrate the changing slopes of the tumor
growth curves over time. Tumor angiogenesis was measured by CD31 staining after the tumor tissues
were removed and made into paraffin sections. We have added a concise analysis of tumor growth rate
variations over time in the Results section, contextualizing the data with key temporal trends and group
comparisons. This revision enhances the interpretive framework by highlighting dynamic growth patterns
relevant to our findings.
We have added the above-mentioned content to the Method section in revised manuscript.
8. The authors suggest that PDLIM5 could be a promising therapeutic target and mention small molecule
inhibitors as a potential strategy. However, there is no experimental data, such as preclinical trials or
efficacy studies, to back up these claims. Including some preliminary studies that explore inhibitors
targeting PDLIM5 or its interaction sites would help demonstrate whether this approach could actually be
effective in a therapeutic setting.
Response: In this study, we validated that PDLIM5 deficiency inhibits the growth of multiple tumors
(including LLC, MC38, and Hepa1-6 subcutaneous xenografts, as well as E0771 orthotopic breast cancer)
using endothelial-specific PDLIM5 knockout mice. We also found that mutant PDLIM5 can suppress tumor
growth. Therefore, we envision that targeting PDLIM5 may serve as a promising anti-angiogenic target.
To further validate PDLIM5 as a potential anti-angiogenic target, we induced genetic deletion of endothelial
PDLIM5 at two distinct therapeutic time windows: the early tumor-bearing stage and after substantial
tumor growth. As demonstrated in Response Figure 4, compared with control groups, both early and
late-stage deletion of endothelial PDLIM5 effectively suppressed the growth of E0771 orthotopic tumors.
Importantly, tumor vascularization was significantly impaired in both groups compared with control, as
evidenced by reduced vascular density. These findings confirm that PDLIM5 inhibition exerts anti-tumor
effects through angiogenesis suppression, regardless of therapeutic initiation timing. We have now
included Response Fig 4 in Fig 2q-u of the revised manuscript.
Notably, our preliminary attempts to develop peptide-based inhibitors mimicking existing strategies for
blocking protein-protein interactions faced technical challenges. Although we synthesized several short
peptides designed to disrupt PDLIM5-ACTN1/ACTN4 binding, their efficacy proved suboptimal. This may
stem from multiple factors including: 1) Insufficient binding specificity of initial peptide designs; 2) Inability
to effectively access the molecular binding pocket between PDLIM5 and ACTN1/ACTN4; 3) Suboptimal
peptide solubility and binding energy parameters. These observations highlight the necessity for
multidisciplinary optimization of molecular design, potentially through computational chemistry
approaches and structural biology-guided modifications.
In light of these findings, we propose that PDLIM5 represents a promising therapeutic target. Future
development of targeted nanomedicines or optimized peptide drugs based on the critical S593/F596
interaction interface could provide viable strategies for PDLIM5-targeted therapies. The technical
challenges encountered in our preliminary peptide development phase underscore the importance of
systematic structure-function studies and advanced drug delivery systems for translating this molecular
target into clinical applications.
Considering that emphasizing PDLIM5 as a valid target without having actually developed small-molecule
inhibitors targeting it could mislead readers, we have revised the relevant descriptions in the abstract and
introduction sections of the paper.

Reviewer #3 (Remarks to the Author):
This paper investigates the role of the cytoskeletal scaffold protein PDLIM5 in promoting angiogenesis by
tumor endothelial cells (TECs). The authors show that PDLIM5 stimulates vascular sprouting in the retina
of healthy mice as well as in tumor grafts. By combining KO of PDLIM5 with anti-PD-L1 treatment, they
further show that this PDLIM5 function can be exploited to decrease tumor growth and promote tumor
immune cell infiltration, suggesting that small molecules directed against PDLIM5 might hold promise as
a new antitumor treatment. To address the mechanism underlying this PDLIM5 function and identify
potential PDLIM5 surfaces to target for drug development, the authors examine the interaction between
PDLIM5 and ACTN1/ACTN4, which has previously been reported in other cell types. In contrast to
Nakagawa et al (2006), they find that PDLIM5 binds to ACTN1/ACTN4 through its Lim domain instead of
its PDZ domain. They further narrow the PDLIM5-ACTN1/4 interaction down to two residues in the third
LIM domain (S593 and F596) and present some data that suggests this interaction enhances the binding
of ACTN1/ACTN4 to F-actin, thereby stabilizing and promoting filopodia formation and angiogenesis. In
line with this, expression of the PDLIM5 double mutant in PDLIM KO mice hampers tumor growth,
angiogenesis and immune cell invasion. The merit of this work mainly lies in the large body of data
supporting PDLIM5 as a potentially interesting antitumor target for a great many different types of cancer.
However, the described underlying mechanism is not fully supported by the data presented. Thus, to
substantiate the claim that this study identified a druggable surface on PDLIM5, the authors will have to
address the issues raised below.
1. Fig. 4: The authors claim that PDLIM5 recruits ACTN1/4 to actin in filopodia, however the linescans
from the images shown in Fig. 4e-f do not show that higher PDLIM5 signals correspond to higher ACTN1/4
signals. In addition, the immunoprecipitation assay in Fig. 4g, shows varying levels of PDLIM5 in WCL,
but does not confirm that this also corresponds to varying levels of PDLIM5 bound to actin after IP.
Hence, they cannot conclude that PDLIM5 regulates the amount of ACTN1/4 bound to actin. To claim that PDLIM5
recruits ACTN1/4 to F-actin, they need to show that the level of PDLIM5 bound to F-actin after
immunoprecipitation changes similarly as the level of ACTN1/4 bound to F-actin after immunoprecipitation.
In addition Line 193: The authors state that PDLIM5 colocalizes with ACTN1/4 in tip cells (Fig. 4e). Are
the cells that are shown in the images and that are used for the linescans actual tip cells?
Response: (a) In Figures 4e-f, we performed immunofluorescence analysis of HUVECs cultured in 2D
confocal dishes for 24 hours. Following phalloidin staining for F-actin and immunostaining for
ACTN1/ACTN4 and PDLIM5, we analyzed the co-localization of these proteins in filopodia structures.
While our initial images may not have optimally demonstrated the tripartite co-localization, higher
magnification revealed concurrent localization of ACTN1/ACTN4, PDLIM5, and F-actin in triangular-
marked protrusions (Fig. 4e-f, as showed in the response Figure 5a-b). We acknowledge that the relatively
weak F-actin signals in some regions might have affected the visual prominence of these protrusions.
Regarding the reviewer's question about whether these cells represent actual tip cells: While 2D-cultured
endothelial cells cannot fully recapitulate native tip cell biology, this established model system remains
valuable for analyzing filopodia-associated protein dynamics. This approach has been successfully
employed in previous angiogenesis studies, including landmark study by De Bock et al. (Cell, 2013). In
their investigation of PFKFB3's role in vessel sprouting, they utilized 2D-cultured GFP-labeled endothelial
cells to demonstrate that PFKFB3 knockdown impaired lamellipodia/filopodia formation and subsequent
endothelial cell sprouting functions, which were further validated through retinal angiogenesis models and
fibrin gel bead assays.
We also conducted additional 3D fibrin gel bead assays using HUVECs (Response Figure 5c-d). These
experiments confirmed co-localization of ACTN1/ACTN4, PDLIM5, and F-actin in filopodia of sprouting tip
cells. While we initially attempted similar experiments with TECs, limited cell yields precluded these
studies. The HUVEC data provide complementary evidence supporting our findings in TECs, consistent
with previous reports demonstrating conserved mechanisms of filopodia formation across endothelial cell
types. We have now included Response Fig 5c-d in Fig S6b-c of the revised manuscript. In fact, the
interaction between PDLIM5 and ACTN4 has been previously reported in cardiac myocytes and skeletal
muscle (Nakagawa, N et al. Biochem Biophys Res Commun. 2000; Wang D, et al. J Cell Mol Med. 2019;
Niederländer Net al. Biochem Biophys Res Commun. 2004), which is consistent with our findings.
(b)To directly address the reviewer's concern, we conducted additional immunoprecipitation (IP)
experiments quantifying PDLIM5-F-actin binding dynamics. Our data demonstrate that PDLIM5
overexpression increases the level of PDLIM5 bound to F-actin, while PDLIM5 knockdown reduces this
interaction compared to controls (Response Figure 5e). These IP results align with our observed changes
in ACTN1/4-F-actin binding (Fig. 4g), showing coordinated regulation of both components. We have now
replaced Fig. 4g with Response Fig 5e in the revised manuscript.

2. Fig 5: The authors should explain why Fig. 5g shows that PDLIM5 mutants bind less ACTN1/4, however
the reverse IP in Fig, 5c-d does not show the same result. Is this perhaps due to the fact that these IP
experiments were performed with full length PDLIM5, which can bind to F-actin and ACTN1/4. The latter
implies that the interpretation of the IP results could be perturbed because there are two binding
interactions to account for, especially given that the authors do not demonstrate that the LIM domain
mutations do not change the overall conformation of PDLIM5 such that it affects its interaction of the
PDZ domain with F-actin. To make matters worse, ACTN1/4 are bone fide F-actin binding proteins,
irrespective of whether their binding is increased by PDLIM5, and thus it should be taken into account that
PDLIM5 binds to F-actin bound by ACTN1/4. To work around this complex situation and avoid any confusion,
the mutant PDLIM5 IP experiments should be repeated with the mutations introduced in the LIM domains only.
This is contrary to Fig. 5h-i. In order to conclude that these mutations fail to recruit ACTN1/4 to F-actin,
the authors should confirm that full length PDLIM5 mutants bind equally well to F-actin as wild type
PDLIM5.
Response：(a) In actuality, Figures 5c-d already indicate a weakened binding of PDLIM5 in the S594A or
F596L mutants. However, the original images suffered from sub-optimal background clarity. We have
repeated the CO-IP experiments to rigorously validate this finding. After observing in Figures 5c-d that
single mutations led to a reduction in the binding affinity between PDLIM5 and ACTN1/ACTN4, we were
motivated to perform double-mutation experiments and subsequent confirmatory studies. In the revised
manuscript, we have replaced the figures with ones that offer a more distinct presentation of the results,
as illustrated in Response Figures 6A-B.
(b) Simultaneously, to more comprehensively verify that PDLIM5 binds to ACTN1/ACTN4 via the
S593/F596 sites within its LIMs domain, we engineered truncated LIMs domain with S593A and F596L
single mutants, as well as the S593A/F596L double mutant. We then employed IP assays to assess the
binding between the LIMs mutants and ACTN1/ACTN4. The data clearly demonstrate that both single
mutations effectively reduce the binding of the LIMs domain to ACTN1/ACTN4, and the double mutation
further diminishes this binding capacity (Response Figure 6C). This strongly suggests that PDLIM5 binds
to ACTN1/ACTN4 through the S593/F596 sites in its LIMs domain. We have now included Response Fig
5C in Fig S8i of the revised manuscript.
(c) Furthermore, we investigated the binding of the mutated PDLIM5 to F-actin. The results reveal that
neither the S593A and F596L single mutations nor the S593A/F596L double mutation of PDLIM5 have a
discernible impact on their binding (Response Figure 6D), and neither the S593A and F596L single
mutations nor the S593A/F596L double mutation of LIMs domain interact with F-actin. We have now
included Response Fig 5D in Fig S8h of the revised manuscript.

Minor comments:
- Include the species of PDLIM5 that was used to clone the lentiviral and adenoviral constructs in the
supplemental methods section.
Response：Thank you for your comments. In our previously submitted manuscript, there were indeed
insufficient methodological details regarding the cloning of PDLIM5. We have now supplemented the
methodology section with the specific species information of the cloned PDLIM5.
- Line 334: Nakagawa et al (2006) also found that the PDLIM5 PDZ domain mediates binding to ACTN1/4.
This difference between their study and this work should be addressed.
Response：First, methodological disparities exist between the two studies. Nakagawa et al. employed
GST-PDZ fusion proteins in pull-down assays with rat heart lysate and C2C12 myogenic cell lysate to
identify PDZ-binding cytoskeletal partners. While their anti-actin immunoblotting demonstrated consistent
F-actin binding across both lysates—aligning with our findings—their anti-α-actinin analysis revealed
tissue-specific interaction: GST-PDZ bound α-actinin (ACTN1/ACTN4) exclusively in rat heart lysate, with
no detectable signal at the expected molecular weight in C2C12 lysate. Notably, the authors provided no
mechanistic rationale for this cell-type dependent discrepancy. Given the inherent challenges of achieving
complete protein extraction from tissues versus cultured cells, compounded by the molecular complexity
of tissue lysates, the methodological validity of this tissue-specific observation remains questionable. In
contrast, our systematic approach addressed these limitations through engineered HA-tagged PDLIM5
variants (full-length, PDZ/LIM domain truncations, and ΔLIM constructs) co-expressed with Myc-tagged
ACTN1 and Flag-tagged ACTN4 in 293T cells. Bidirectional co-immunoprecipitation confirmed LIM
domain-dependent binding, while structure-guided mutagenesis (S593A, F596L, and S593A/F596L
double mutant) localized the interaction interface to residues S593/F596 within the LIM domains, as
validated in Response Figure 6C. This integrative strategy—combining domain mapping with residue-
level mutagenesis—provides robust structural evidence that PDLIM5 engages ACTN1/ACTN4 via
S593/F596 residues in its LIM domains. Technical enhancements including explicit epitope tagging
(HA/Myc/Flag), cellular system specification (293T), methodological distinction between pull-down and
CO-IP systems, and standardized structural terminology collectively strengthen scientific rigor while
respectfully contextualizing prior findings.
- It would be nice of the authors could expand the discussion a bit to also talk about how the PDLIM-
actinin interaction is required for the other PDLIM family members.
Response：We sincerely thank the reviewer for this important suggestion. The interaction with α-actinin
appears to be a conserved yet functionally diversified feature across multiple PDLIM family members,
extending beyond the previously emphasized roles of PDLIM5/7 and PDLIM1. While PDLIM1 selectively
binds α-actinin4 (ACTN4) at Asn145 to suppress F-actin overgrowth and sustain Hippo signaling via
LATS1 stabilization (Huang Z, et al. Hepatology. 2020), Pdlim2 interacts broadly with α-actinins to regulate
cytoskeletal stability (Sistani L, et al. Kidney Int. 2011; Torrado M, et al. Invest Ophthalmol Vis Sci. 2004),
suggesting isoform-specific partnerships fine-tuned for distinct cellular outputs. Similarly, PDLIM5/7 not
only recruit YAP via their PDZ domain but also rely on direct α-actinin binding to translocate to stress
fibers under mechanical force, thereby coupling cytoskeletal tension to YAP activation (Elbediwy A, et al.
J Cell Sci. 2018). This recurring theme—where LIM domains engage α-actinins to scaffold cytoskeletal
organization, while PDZ domains either anchor to F-actin or recruit signaling effectors (e.g., YAP)—implies
that α-actinin interactions are integral to the PDLIM family’s dual role as mechanosensitive adaptors. Such
functional conservation highlights α-actinin as a central node enabling PDLIM proteins to spatially
integrate cytoskeletal dynamics with pathway-specific signaling, a mechanism likely critical for all family
members despite context-dependent variations in binding partners or downstream targets. We have
added the relevant content to the discussion section of the revised manuscript.
Reviewer #4 (Remarks to the Author):
In the study entitled “Endothelial PDLIM5 promotes tip cell filopodia formation and tumor angiogenesis by
regulating ACTN1/ACTN4-dependent actin bundling”, the authors investigate the role of PDZ and LIM
domain 5 (PDLIM5) in tumor endothelial cell (TEC)-mediated angiogenesis. They demonstrate that
PDLIM5 is highly expressed in lung cancer TECs, correlates with poor patient survival, and plays a crucial
role in filopodia formation by interacting with actinin-1/actinin-4 (ACTN1/ACTN4) to facilitate filamentous
actin (F-actin) bundling. Endothelial-specific deletion of PDLIM5 disrupts sprouting angiogenesis, reduces
tumor growth, normalizes tumor vasculature, and enhances immunotherapy response in resistant tumors.
These findings suggest that PDLIM5 may serve as a novel therapeutic target to improve cancer treatment
outcomes.
Comments:
The results presented in the manuscript provide substantial evidence on the role of PDLIM5 in TECs and
its potential impact on tumor angiogenesis. However, a number of comments should be addressed to
support the claims and findings presented in the manuscript. These include:
1. Additional functional studies are needed to convincingly demonstrate that endothelial PDLIM5 regulates
tip cell function. For instance, in vitro migration assays and competition sprouting assays, where a mixed
population WT and PDLIM5-silenced cells compete for the tip cell position, could provide additional
strength.
It would be also important to investigate how the tip cell subset (as well as the additional subtypes) is
affected in the endothelial-specific PDLIM5 KO in mice.
Response：(a) We sincerely appreciate the reviewer's suggestions. The proposed in vitro migration and
competitive sprouting assays are indeed pivotal for elucidating PDLIM5's role in tip cell function. Therefore,
we first performed scratch assays on PDLIM5 knockdown and wild-type endothelial cells. Results showed
that PDLIM5 knockdown significantly inhibited migration in endothelial cells in a tranwell migration model.
Additionally, we conducted competition sprouting assays using lenti-GFP-labeled wild-type cells and lenti-
RFP-labeled PDLIM5 knockdown endothelial cells. Quantitative analysis revealed that wild-type cells
dominated sprouting structures in tip cell formation compared to PDLIM5-deficient counterparts
(Response Figure 7A-B). We have now included Response Fig 7B in Fig S8h of the revised manuscript.
(b) We sincerely thank the reviewer for their insightful comments. Investigating the impact of PDLIM5
deletion on tumor endothelial subsets (e.g., tip cells) is critical for understanding its angiogenesis
regulatory mechanisms. Given the complex experimental workflows and analysis pipelines required for
single-cell sequencing, we employed flow cytometry to sort CD31+ endothelial cell populations and used
qPCR to quantify mRNA expression levels of key tip cell markers (including CXCR4, ESM1, and DLL4).
These genes have been validated as specific tip cell markers in multiple studies (Zhoufeng Wang et al.
Nat Commun. 2021; Xudong Xing et al. Sci Adv. 2021; Yi-Feng Ren et al. Mol Cancer. 2024; Yilv Yan et
al. Nat Genet. 2025), with their expression dynamics effectively reflecting tip cell activation status. We
have successfully established an endothelial cell sorting system, and preliminary data show significant
downregulation of these markers in PDLIM5 KO mice (Response Figure 7C). This result aligns with our
previously submitted RNA-seq data in HUVECs. While this approach has slightly lower resolution than
single-cell sequencing, its targeted analysis provides direct evidence for subset functional differences.
We will highlight the correlation between these findings and vascular phenotypic abnormalities in the
discussion section and plan to perform spatial transcriptomic analysis in future studies for further validation.
We have now included Response Fig 7C in Fig S5C of the revised manuscript.
Response Figure 7. (A) Transwell migration assay detects the migration ability of WT vs PDLIM5 KD
HUVECs. (B) Representative image and quantification of sprouts from the fibrin gel sprouting assay with
1:1 competitive seeding of WT (Green) and PDLIM5 KD (red) HUVECs on the beads. Scale bar, 100 μm.
Data are presented as mean with SD. Unpaired t test. ***, p< 0.001. (C) Relative mRNA expression of
PDLIM5 and tipEC markers (CXCR4, ESM1, DLL4) and MMP2 were analyzed in TECs isolated from
PDLIM5f/f (n=3) or PDLIM5cKO (n=3) mice. Data are presented as mean with SD. Unpaired t test. ***, p<
0.001.
2. While the authors propose that endothelial PDLIM5 deletion induces tumor vessel normalization (TVN),
Figure 2 suggests vessel pruning (reduced vessel density), which is likely responsible for the observed
reduced tumor growth. This discrepancy warrants an explanation. TVN is often associated with improved
metastasis outcomes rather than with an effect on primary tumor growth. It would be useful to investigate
the relationship between vessel pruning and reduced tumor growth and explore whether TVN by PDLIM5
deletion affects metastasis.
Response：(a) We sincerely appreciate your meticulous review and the valuable questions you've raised.
Regarding the potential discrepancy you've pointed out between the vessel pruning (manifested as
decreased vessel density) shown in Figure 2 and our proposed induction of tumor vessel normalization
(TVN) by endothelial PDLIM5 deletion, the following is our explanation.
Tumor vessel normalization is an intricate process, not a simple, single alteration. Conventionally, vessel
normalization has often been narrowly regarded as the optimization of vascular structure and function
without significant reduction in vessel quantity. However, in the context of the tumor microenvironment,
vessel pruning is indeed an integral part of the vessel normalization process. When endothelial PDLIM5
is depleted, it triggers a cascade of molecular and cellular events. Initially, the functional state of vascular
endothelial cells is altered, compelling the remodeling of the chaotic, abnormally branched, and inefficient
tumor vascular system. During this remodeling, poorly perfused and malfunctioning vascular branches
are gradually pruned away, which is precisely what is reflected by the reduced vessel density in Figure 2,
Figure 7 and Supplemental Figure 10. This pruning is not an isolated phenomenon separate from vessel
normalization; rather, it represents a crucial manifestation of normalization. By eliminating these non-
functional vascular branches, the remaining vessels can re-distribute blood flow, enhancing the delivery
of oxygen and nutrients, which lies at the heart of the functionality of vessel normalization. Additionally,
vessel normalization also encompasses aspects such as the improvement of pericytes coverage and the
reconstruction of the basement membrane. Collectively, these elements form the comprehensive
landscape of tumor vessel normalization, and many previous studies also support this view (Tian L, et al.
Nature. 2017; Huang Y, et al. Nat Rev Immunol. 2018; Lu Z, et al. Sci Transl Med. 2024; Augustin HG,
Koh GY. Cancer Res. 2022). The observed slowdown in tumor growth in our study is precisely the outcome
of the optimization of the tumor microenvironment and the transformation of its supportive effect on tumor
cells following vessel normalization, which includes this vessel-pruning step.
(b) Regarding whether PDLIM5 knockout affects tumor metastasis, we conducted relevant investigations.
We established subcutaneous LLC tumor xenografts, performed surgical resection of primary tumors, and
analyzed lung metastasis after tumor regrowth. This method has been validated previously to successfully
establish lung metastasis models (Lu Z, et al. Sci Transl Med. 2024). Results showed that PDLIM5 deletion
significantly inhibited LLC lung metastasis (Response Figure 8A). We have now included Response Fig
8A-C in Fig S11A-C of the revised manuscript.
While the reviewer noted that "TVN is often associated with improved metastasis outcomes," conflicting
evidence exists. For example, Elena Magrini et al. (2014) demonstrated that endothelial L1 deficiency
reduced tumor angiogenesis and promoted vessel normalization. In Panc02 tumor-bearing L1floxed vs.
Tie2-Cre;L1floxed mice, metastasis incidence was 5/7 (71%) vs. 2/7 (29%), with fewer site-specific
metastases in Tie2-Cre;L1floxed mice (Magrini et al. J Clin Invest. 2014). Similarly, Anna Rita Cantelmo
and Silvia La Porta reported that endothelial-specific deletion of PFKFB3 or Tie1 reduces B16-F10 and
LLC lung metastasis, attributing this phenomenon to the notion that "normalized vasculature constitutes
a tighter endothelial barrier, rendering tumor cells less prone to escape." (Cantelmo et al. Cancer Cell.
2016; La Porta S, et al. J Clin Invest. 2018). These findings align with numerous studies and reviews
supporting the concept that vessel normalization reduces metastasis. In our study, we propose that
PDLIM5 deletion reduces primary tumor metastasis by promoting vascular normalization.
Response Figure 8. (A) Schematic diagram showing the establishment of a pulmonary metastasis model
via subcutaneous tumor xenograft. LLC cells were injected subcutaneously, and once tumors reached 1.5
cm in diameter, the overlying skin was incised to excise the tumor mass in day 15. After wound suturing,
mice were allowed to recover and continue to be raised. After 3 weeks lung tissues were harvested for
fixation and histological analysis. (B) Representative H&E staining images of mouse lung tissues, with
yellow arrows indicating pulmonary metastatic foci. Scale bar, 1 mm. (C) Quantitative analysis of the
number of pulmonary metastatic foci. Data are presented as mean with SD. Unpaired t test. ***, p< 0.001.
3. The mechanism by which endothelial PDLIM5 regulates T cell infiltration needs further investigations.
Are increased T cell infiltration levels due to enhanced delivery upon TVN, or is there an effect on adhesion
molecules? ICAM-1 clustering and function has been shown to be directly linked to ACTN4 (Celli et al. J
Immunol. 2006). Thus, it would be crucial to assess whether PDLIM5 deletion alters ICAM-1 clustering.
Additionally, as actin-binding proteins can differentially regulate EC stiffness (Schaefer, et al. J Cell 2014),
it would be valuable to investigate whether PDLIM5 deletion leads to changes in EC stiffness that might
favor T cell transmigration.
Response：In Figure 7 and Supplemental Figure 10, we mainly demonstrate that PDLIM5 deficiency
promotes tumor vascular normalization (including increased pericyte coverage, enhanced perfusion levels,
and reduced permeability). The normalized tumor vasculature also alleviates tumor hypoxia. Previous
studies have shown that normalized tumor vasculature can enhance immunotherapy efficacy, as
evidenced by clinical observations that anti-angiogenic therapy combined with immunotherapy prolongs
survival in various cancers (Schoenfeld JD, et al. Lancet Oncol. 2022; Reardon DA, et al. JAMA Oncol.
2020; Yuan L, et al. Nat Commun. 2023; Adkins D, et al. Lancet Oncol. 2024).
In our previous version, we did not sufficiently explain why PDLIM5 deficiency promotes T-cell infiltration.
We hypothesized that vascular normalization might facilitate T-cell infiltration without exploring the specific
mechanisms. Indeed, many previous studies have found that normalized tumor vessels enhance T-cell
infiltration and antitumor immunity through structural and functional remodeling (Tian L, et al. Nature. 2017;
Huang Y, et al. Nat Rev Immunol. 2018; Lu Z, et al. Sci Transl Med. 2024; Augustin HG, Koh GY. Cancer
Res. 2022). First, vascular normalization restores vessel architecture by stabilizing the basement
membrane and aligning endothelial cells, reducing vascular leakage and improving blood perfusion. This
optimization of hemodynamics enables efficient delivery of T cells to tumors while alleviating hypoxia,
which suppresses immunosuppressive factors such as HIF-1α and reduces the recruitment of regulatory
Tregulatory
T cells (Tregs) and myeloid-derived suppressor cells (MDSCs). Second, normalized endothelial cells
upregulate adhesion molecules (e.g., ICAM-1, VCAM-1) to facilitate T-cell adhesion and transmigration,
guided by chemotactic gradients of CXCL9, CXCL10, and CXCL16. Collectively, these mechanisms
synergistically enhance T-cell trafficking and infiltration into the tumor microenvironment.
Regarding whether PDLIM5 deficiency affects ICAM1 and cell stiffness, we also conducted analysis. The
results showed that PDLIM5 deficiency promotes ICAM1 aggregation on endothelial cell membranes and
reduces cell stiffness (Response Figure 9).
Knockdown of PDLIM5 could increase the aggregation of ICAM1 on the membrane (Response Figure
9A). The reviewer also mentioned that Celli et al. found that ICAM-1 directly interacts with cytoplasmic α-
actinin 1 and 4, and that this interaction is required for leukocyte extravasation, and α-actinin 4 had a
major role in this phenomenon (Celli et al. J Immunol. 2006). In this study, the authors identified three
amino acids (arginine 480, 486, and lysine 481) that were critical in the ICAM-1 interaction with both α-
actinins, suggesting that α-actinins bind to the same amino acids on ICAM-1. Actually, even earlier,
Carpén et al. also found that the region of ICAM-1, 478-505, interacting with α-actinin was mapped to the area
close to the membrane-spanning region. At the same time, they found that the interaction appeared to be
sensitive to an increase in ionic strength. When the molarity of NaCl was raised from 0.15 to 0.3 M or
above, the interaction was markedly reduced or totally abolished. They wrote in the discussion that “The
interaction was partially dependent on divalent cation concentration, which is of interest since the COOH-
terminal region of α-actinin contains two EF hand-like calcium-binding motifs” (Carpén et al. J Cell Biol.
1992). And these two EF hand-like calcium-binding motifs are also crucial for the binding of α-actinin to
F-actin. In 1987, Noegel et al. found that when the calcium ion concentration increased, the two EF hand-
like calcium-binding motifs of α-actinin would bind to calcium ions, thus releasing the binding to F-actin
(Noegel et al. FEBS Letters. 1987). Combining with our research findings, PDLIM5 binds to the EF hand-
like calcium-binding motifs of α-actinin through the LIMs domain and binds to F-actin through the PDZ
domain. We speculate that when the calcium ion concentration increases, the binding between PDLIM5
and α-actinin will be blocked, thereby reducing the binding of α-actinin to F-actin. At the same time,
combining with the findings of Carpén et al., we hypothesis that PDLIM5 may competitively bind to the EF
hand-like calcium-binding motifs of α-actinin with ICAM1. So, after the knockdown of PDLIM5, the binding
between ICAM1 and α-actinin increases, which promotes the aggregation of ICAM1 on the cell membrane.
To verify this, we detected the interaction between ACTN4 and ICAM1 in PDLIM5 knockdown cells, we
found that after the knockdown of PDLIM5, the binding between ACTN1/ACTN4 and ICAM1 increased
(Response Figure 9B). In addition, we isolated primary pulmonary endothelial cells from mice and CD3+

knockdown of PDLIM5 also reduced cell stiffness (Response Figure 9D). Based on this, we believe that
the deletion of PDLIM5 promotes the clustering of ICAM1 on the cell membrane, which in turn increases
T-cell adhesion and trans-endothelial transport. We have now included Response Fig 9A-F in Fig 7d-i of
the revised manuscript.

T-cell trans-endothelial migration. Moreover, other vascular normalization phenotypes induced by PDLIM5
deficiency (including increased pericyte coverage, enhanced perfusion levels, and reduced permeability)

Response: Regarding whether PDLIM5 promotes tumor angiogenesis through regulating NO release.
First, NO release increases in endothelial cells during eNOS activation. In 2003, Jean-Philippe Gratton et
al. found that in LLC subcutaneous tumor models, tumors in eNOS−/− mice showed reduced Evans blue
permeability compared to wild-type mice. More importantly, tumor progression was significantly attenuated
in eNOS−/− mice versus LLC-implanted wild-type mice, accompanied by decreased PECAM-1-positive
vascular density (6.6% ± 0.4% vs. 3.5% ± 0.7* % PECAM-1-positive density, *p < 0.05; n = 4 per group).
These results indicate that inhibiting NO production suppresses tumor growth and angiogenesis. Evidence
also shows tumor cells induce endothelial NO release to enhance vascular permeability. VEGF-induced
vascular leakage is abolished in eNOS-deficient mice or wild-type mice treated with NOS inhibitors like L-
NAME (Fukumura et al., 2001; Murohara et al., 1998a). Thus, NO promotes tumor growth and increases
vascular permeability. However, our previous studies revealed that PDLIM5 expression increases during
mechanical vascular injury, inhibiting AKT activation and subsequent eNOS phosphorylation, thereby
reducing NO release. Endothelial PDLIM5 knockout in endothelial cells increased eNOS phosphorylation
and NO release, impairing vascular remodeling, suggesting PDLIM5 acts as a negative regulator of the
eNOS/NO pathway (Huang et al., Arterioscler Thromb Vasc Biol. 2020). In this study, PDLIM5 deficiency
suppressed tumor growth, angiogenesis, and vascular permeability while enhancing T cell infiltration. If
PDLIM5 functions through NO regulation, PDLIM5 deletion promotes NO release (Response Figure 10),
thereby accelerating tumor growth, angiogenesis, and vascular permeability – contradicting Gratton et
al.'s findings in eNOS−/− mice. Therefore, we conclude that PDLIM5-mediated tumor angiogenesis and
post-knockout tumor vessel normalization are independent of NO regulation.
Regarding Hiroi Y et al.'s research, they identified direct interaction between α-actinin-4 and eNOS: full-

eNOS activity, with α-actinin-4 loss in BAECs increasing eNOS activity (Hiroi Y et al., FASEB J. 2008).
However, evidence for PDLIM5-α-actinin-4 interaction regulating eNOS in tumor endothelium remains
limited. Our prior work demonstrated PDLIM5 primarily modulates eNOS phosphorylation through AKT
signaling.
In this study, we screened PDLIM5-binding proteins ACTN1/ACTN4 through mass spectrometry analysis
and characterized the mechanism of PDLIM5 interaction with ACTN1/ACTN4 at the molecular and cellular
functional levels , as well as its impact on filopodia formation in tip cells (Figure 4-6, Figure S6-S9). Further,
in the in vivo rescue phenotype assay, reintroducing PDLIM5 mutation failed to rescue the inhibitory effects
of PDLIM5 deficiency on tumor growth and angiogenesis (Figure 6e-j), strongly demonstrating that
PDLIM5 promotes angiogenesis by binding to ACTN1/ACTN4.

Reviewer #5 (Remarks to the Author):
(General comments)
This study investigates the role of endothelial PDLIM5, an actin binding cytoskeletal protein with PDZ and
LIM domain 4, in tumor angiogenesis. The authors demonstrate that PDLIM5 is highly expressed in tumor
endothelial cells (TECs) in lung cancer, correlating with poor patient survival. Mechanistically, PDLIM5
promotes tumor angiogenesis by interaction with ACTN1/ACTN4 via its S693/F596 residues, facilitating
F-actin bundling and tip cell filopodia formation. Using EC-specific PDLIM5 KO mice, the study shows that
loss of PDLIM5 not only suppresses tumor growth but also improves tumor vascular function, reduces
intratumoral hypoxia, enhances T cell infiltration, and increases the efficacy of immune checkpoint
inhibitors (anti-PD-LI antibody treatment). The experiments from Figure 1 to Figure 6 are well designed
and demonstrate the role of PDLIM5 in promoting tip cell filopodia formation and tumor angiogenesis via
interaction with ACTN1/ACTN4 via S693/F596 using PDLIM5 KD cells and KO mice knocked in with either
adeno-WT or S588A/F591L mutant PDLIM5.
However, there are two major concerns with this study:
1) Figure 7 does not integrate well with the rest of the study, as it shifts the focus to CD8+ and CD4+T
cells in LLC tumors from WT or PDLIM5 KO mice in the context of immune checkpoint inhibitors therapy;
Response：Given that this major concern essentially aligns with Major Comment 2, I aim to offer a unified
response here and earnestly hope for the reviewer's comprehension
In our previous submission, the description of the research purpose for Figure 7 might have given readers
the impression of deviating from the main research focus, with insufficient logical rigor. We have revised
this section accordingly.
It is necessary to clarify why we conducted the studies related to Figures 7 and 8. The primary objective
of this study was to investigate the role and mechanism of PDLIM5 in tumor angiogenesis. While PDLIM5
deficiency inhibits tumor angiogenesis, it also exerts functional impacts on tumor vasculature. Therefore,
in Figure 7, we explored whether PDLIM5 deficiency affects tumor vascular perfusion levels and
permeability while blocking angiogenesis, and whether it improves the tumor microenvironment,
particularly in terms of its potential influence on cancer immunotherapy.
In Figure 7 and Supplemental Figure 10, we mainly demonstrate that PDLIM5 deficiency promotes tumor
vascular normalization (including increased pericyte coverage, enhanced perfusion levels, and reduced
permeability). The normalized tumor vasculature also alleviates tumor hypoxia. Previous studies have
shown that normalized tumor vasculature can enhance immunotherapy efficacy, as evidenced by clinical
observations that anti-angiogenic therapy combined with immunotherapy prolongs survival in various
cancers (Schoenfeld JD, et al. Lancet Oncol. 2022; Reardon DA, et al. JAMA Oncol. 2020; Yuan L, et al.
Nat Commun. 2023; Adkins D, et al. Lancet Oncol. 2024). Therefore, we further investigated whether
PDLIM5, as a potential anti-angiogenic target, could sensitize tumors to immunotherapy.
In our previous version, we did not sufficiently explain why PDLIM5 deficiency promotes T-cell infiltration.
We hypothesized that vascular normalization might facilitate T-cell infiltration without exploring the specific
mechanisms. Indeed, many previous studies have found that normalized tumor vessels enhance T-cell
infiltration and antitumor immunity through structural and functional remodeling (Tian L, et al. Nature. 2017;
Huang Y, et al. Nat Rev Immunol. 2018; Lu Z, et al. Sci Transl Med. 2024; Augustin HG, Koh GY. Cancer
Res. 2022). First, vascular normalization restores vessel architecture by stabilizing the basement
membrane and aligning endothelial cells, reducing vascular leakage and improving blood perfusion. This
optimization of hemodynamics enables efficient delivery of T cells to tumors while alleviating hypoxia,
which suppresses immunosuppressive factors such as HIF-1α and reduces the recruitment of regulatory
T cells (Tregs) and myeloid-derived suppressor cells (MDSCs). Second, normalized endothelial cells
upregulate adhesion molecules (e.g., ICAM-1, VCAM-1) to facilitate T-cell adhesion and transmigration,
guided by chemotactic gradients of CXCL9, CXCL10, and CXCL16. Collectively, these mechanisms
synergistically enhance T-cell trafficking and infiltration into the tumor microenvironment.
Other reviewers also have raised questions about potential changes in endothelial cell expression of T-
cell adhesion molecules (e.g., ICAM1) and alterations in cellular stiffness. So, we also examined the
effects of PDLIM5 deficiency on ICAM1 and cell stiffness. The results demonstrated that PDLIM5
deficiency promotes ICAM1 aggregation on endothelial cell membranes and reduces cell stiffness
(Response Figure 9). These factors are all conducive to promoting T-cell trans-endothelial migration.
Given that we possess endothelial-specific PDLIM5 knockout mice, we further explored whether PDLIM5
deficiency could enhance tumor immunotherapy by increasing T-cell infiltration. The results in Figure 8
demonstrate that PDLIM5 deficiency synergizes with immune checkpoint inhibitors. We believe Figures 7
and 8 hold significant implications, as these findings provide theoretical foundations and fundamental data
for future translational research on PDLIM5-targeted anti-tumor therapies.
2) Previous study (PMID:29228678) shows that PDLIM5 promotes tumor cell proliferation, invasion and
migration via binding to AMPK. However, the potential interaction between PDLIM5 and AMPK in TECs
has not been investigated in this study. These issues should be addressed.
Response: Given that this major concern essentially aligns with Major Comment 3, I aim to offer a unified
response here and earnestly hope for the reviewer's comprehension
First, the activation of AMPK by basic fibroblast growth factor (bFGF), adiponectin, hypoxia, and VEGF is
critically involved in angiogenesis. Notably, dominant-negative AMPK mutants have been shown to
suppress endothelial cell migration toward VEGF and inhibit in vitro tube formation under hypoxic
conditions (Fisslthaler et al., Circ Res. 2009; Levine et al., J Biol Chem. 2007), supporting the pro-
migratory role of AMPK in endothelial cells.
Regarding the study cited by the reviewer (PMID: 29228678), which reported that PDLIM5 promotes tumor
cell proliferation, invasion, and migration by binding to AMPK, we note that the authors demonstrated
PDLIM5 interaction with AMPK reduces its ubiquitination-dependent degradation, thereby enhancing
prostate cancer cell migration. This aligns with earlier work in mouse C2C12 myofibroblasts showing that
Pdlim5 directly binds AMPK via its LIM domain and facilitates AMPK recruitment to F-actin through α-
actinin (Yan et al., Nat Commun. 2014).
To clarify potential cell type-specific mechanisms, we investigated PDLIM5-AMPK interaction and its
functional consequences in HUVECs. Our data demonstrate that PDLIM5 physically interacts with AMPK
in HUVECs. PDLIM5 knockdown Inhibits AMPK phosphorylation (activation), but does not alter total
AMPK protein levels, suggesting that PDLIM5 does not regulate AMPK ubiquitination or stability in
endothelial cells (Response Figure 12). In summary, our findings suggest that the reduced AMPK
activation upon PDLIM5 knockdown in HUVECs is secondary to filopodia dysfunction and altered energy
demands, rather than direct regulation of AMPK stability. This highlights context-dependent roles of
PDLIM5-AMPK interaction across cell types.
In this study, we screened PDLIM5-binding proteins ACTN1/ACTN4 through mass spectrometry analysis
in HUVECs, and AMPK are not included. Then we characterized the mechanism of PDLIM5 interaction
with ACTN1/ACTN4 at the molecular and cellular functional levels, as well as its impact on filopodia
formation in tip cells (Figure 4-6, Figure S6-S9). Further, in the in vivo rescue phenotype assay,
reintroducing PDLIM5 mutation failed to rescue the inhibitory effects of PDLIM5 deficiency on tumor
growth and angiogenesis (Figure 6e-j), strongly demonstrating that PDLIM5 promotes angiogenesis by
binding to ACTN1/ACTN4.
We propose the following mechanism: 1) PDLIM5 deficiency disrupts filopodia formation, impairing cell
migration. This reduced migratory activity may lower cellular energy demand, thereby decreasing AMPK
activation. 2) Filopodia formation requires ATP-driven actin polymerization. Abnormal filopodia dynamics
(e.g., excessive or insufficient protrusion) could perturb local ATP/AMP ratios, indirectly modulating AMPK
sensing of energy status. Whether PDLIM5 inhibits the migration of tumor endothelial cells by regulating
AMPK activity requires further comprehensive studies in the future.

REVIEWER COMMENTS
Reviewer #1 (Remarks to the Author):
1. In this revision, the authors have addressed most of my comments and corrected the errors found
in the figures. Regarding annotating all the rest of non-arterial/venus/capillary/lymphatic ECs as
TipECs, my concern still remains. Tip ECs are referred to a very specific type of endothelial cells.
Since the authors have referred to reference 5, as well as reanalyzing the data from reference 5,
there are far more heterogeneity of EC phenotypes based on the single cell RNA sequencing profiles,
also found in reference 5. Tip cells are one of the tumor-enriched EC phenotypes. What about other
EC phenotypes found in TECs, such as immature ECs, proliferating ECs? Using the term of Tip Cells
will substantially mislead the readers. If the study could not classify this cluster ECs into further sub-
phenotyping, another term rather TipECs should be used, for example it would be “tumor-enriched
ECs”, which exhibit increased expression of immunomodulating, tip cells and proliferating endothelial
cells signature.
Response: We sincerely appreciate the reviewer's insightful comments regarding endothelial cell
(EC) heterogeneity within the tumor microenvironment (TME) and the specific concern about using
the term "tip ECs" to annotate the cluster of non-arterial/venous/capillary/lymphatic ECs. We fully
agree with the reviewer that tumor endothelial cells (TECs) exhibit significant phenotypic diversity,
encompassing not only tip cells but also immature and proliferating ECs, as elegantly demonstrated
in reference 5 and other studies.
As illustrated in Response Figure 1, our initial attempt to replicate the precise 11-subcluster
classification from reference 5 was hindered by critical technical differences. Since our ECs were
identified from whole-tissue dissociations without CD31/CD45 pre-sorting, the total number was
relatively low (~1,900 total ECs, with 863 TECs), compared to the pre-enriched ~21,000 ECs
analyzed in reference 5. Applying reference 5's approach as closely as possible, we classified our
ECs into 7 subtypes: Arterial ECs, Lymphatic ECs, Activated Postcapillary Vein ECs, Postcapillary
Venous ECs, Tip Cells, Type I Alveolar Capillary ECs, and Type II Alveolar Capillary ECs. We were
unable to further resolve the immature ECs and proliferating ECs subtypes mentioned by the
reviewer. Importantly, the "Tip Cells" cluster identified this way aligned perfectly with the "tip ECs"
cluster from our original manuscript, and the observation of its increased proportion in TECs
remained consistent.
Faced with these practical limitations in resolving the full spectrum of EC heterogeneity, we adopted
the widely utilized and pragmatic five-category classification (Arterial, Venous, Capillary, Lymphatic,
Tip) prevalent in numerous published tumor scRNA-seq studies (e.g., Qiu J et al., Adv Sci 2023; Li
J et al., Natl Sci Rev 2024; Pu W et al., Nat Commun 2021; Zhang J et al., Comput Struct Biotechnol
J 2022; Xie Z et al., Cell Mol Life Sci 2024). This approach provided a robust and reproducible
framework for analyzing PDLIM5 expression across major EC compartments within the constraints
of our dataset.
The reviewer suggests that our "tip ECs" cluster might encompass cells like immature ECs and
proliferating ECs due to shared biological functions (e.g., high proliferative and migratory capacity),
and proposes renaming this group "tumor-enriched ECs, which exhibit increased expression of
immunomodulating, tip cells and proliferating endothelial cells signature." We understand the desire
for a more refined and specialized description for readers. However, we are concerned that "tumor-
enriched ECs" is a relatively newer and broader term that may not intuitively convey the specific
functional phenotype to all readers, especially those outside the tumor vasculature field. In contrast,
the classification into "Arterial (A), Venous (V), Capillary (Cap), Lymphatic (L), and Tip (T)"
ECs
represents a long-established, fundamental paradigm in vascular biology that is widely understood
and accepted. Using "Tip ECs" clearly communicates the core biological characteristics of this
cluster—enrichment for classic tip cell markers and association with migration/sprouting functions—
to a broad audience, including non-tumor vascular biology experts.
Furthermore, to directly address the reviewer's concerns about heterogeneity and other tumor
endothelial phenotypes, and to validate using the gold-standard reference, we re-analyzed the public
dataset from reference 5. As shown in Response Figure 1E (to be included as Supplementary Figure
2G and described in the Results section), PDLIM5 expression was significantly higher in TECs vs.
NECs specifically within the following subclusters: "tip cell", "artery ECs", "immature ECs", and
"Activated Postcapillary Vein ECs". This result confirms PDLIM5 upregulation across multiple tumor-
associated activated endothelial phenotypes, supporting the concept of TEC heterogeneity. Despite
this heterogeneity, the "tip cell" subcluster exhibited one of the most significant upregulations of
PDLIM5, and its core function (migration) is precisely the key function of PDLIM5 validated by our
functional experiments. These experiments conclusively demonstrate PDLIM5's contribution to
promoting migration—the core function of tip cells.
Regarding immature ECs: We fully acknowledge the importance of immature ECs and other
phenotypes highlighted by the reviewer. Indeed, our re-analysis of reference 5 data confirmed
significant PDLIM5 upregulation in the "immature ECs" subcluster. We will incorporate a detailed
discussion of this point in the manuscript. It is noteworthy that immature ECs typically display high
proliferative and migratory potential, along with immunomodulatory properties. There is considerable
overlap in gene expression profiles and functional characteristics (e.g., high migratory capacity)
between immature ECs and tip cells. While scRNA-seq can distinguish them transcriptionally, their
biological functions in promoting angiogenesis are likely closely related or exist on a continuum.
Therefore, PDLIM5 upregulation in immature ECs further underscores its role in a broader
"activated/pro-angiogenic endothelial state." Tip cells, representing the most migratory vanguard
within this state, served as the ideal entry point for our functional investigation. Our functional data
demonstrating PDLIM5's pro-migratory role is equally relevant to understanding its function in highly
migratory cell types, including immature ECs.
Regarding the proportion of tip cells: We note that in reference 5, the tip cell proportion ranged from
0.75% to 37.30%, with an average of 9.44% across seven patients, despite their finer subclustering,
highlighting substantial inter-individual variability. In our samples, the proportion of tip ECs in lung
cancer tissues also showed significant variation, ranging from ~18% to 50% (Response Figure 1F).
In summary: While our scRNA-seq dataset itself may lack the resolution to definitively resolve
immature ECs, proliferating ECs, etc., even when attempting finer classification into 7 subtypes, the
identity and proportion of the tip cell cluster remained unchanged. This suggests a high degree of
similarity in gene expression and cellular function within this cluster, consistent with the shared high
proliferative/migratory functions of tip cells, immature ECs, and proliferating ECs. Considering that
"tumor-enriched ECs" is a relatively new and potentially less intuitive term for the specific functional
phenotype to a broad readership, we believe retaining the established five-category classification (A,
V, Cap, L, Tip) is preferable. We will explicitly acknowledge the limitations of this classification
approach in our Discussion section. We hope this explanation and our planned revisions adequately
address the reviewer's concerns and that retaining the "tip cell" terminology will enhance clarity for
readers. We thank the reviewer again for their valuable feedback.

2. The authors mention "a supportive effect of TME optimization on tumor cells following vessel
normalization". However, this concept is unclear, how is the supportive effect exerted, and what does
it imply? Clarification is needed.
Response: We sincerely appreciate the reviewer's insightful question regarding the phrase "The
observed slowdown in tumor growth in our study is precisely the outcome of the optimization of the
tumor microenvironment and the transformation of its supportive effect on tumor cells following
vessel normalization, which includes this vessel-pruning step" in our previous response. We
acknowledge that this wording lacked sufficient clarity and could be misinterpreted. We apologize
for any confusion caused and provide the following detailed explanation: (1) By "supportive effect of
the TME," we refer to the collective physical and biochemical conditions within the tumor
microenvironment that objectively enable or facilitate tumor cell survival, proliferation, invasion, and
metastasis. This includes, but is not limited to, nutrient and oxygen supply, waste removal, growth
factor signaling, immune evasion mechanisms, and the physical scaffold provided by the
extracellular matrix and vasculature. Crucially, this is a functional description of the TME's state, not
implying a beneficial outcome for the host.
The key point we intended to convey is that endothelial PDLIM5 deletion-induced vessel
normalization fundamentally alters the quality and functional consequences of this TME support.
Specifically, it triggers a shift from a pro-tumorigenic, pathological support to a less supportive, more
normalized, and ultimately anti-tumorigenic environment, including improving perfusion and
alleviating hypoxia (removing a key driver of tumor aggression), reducing acidosis and enhancing
immune cell infiltration (promoting anti-tumor immunity), pruning dysfunctional vessels (diminishing
routes for metastasis). Collectively, these changes transform the TME from a pro-tumorigenic
environment into one that is restrictive to tumor growth and dissemination.
Therefore, the "optimization" and "transformation" we described do not imply that the normalized
TME enhances support for tumor cells. On the contrary, by mitigating key drivers of tumor
progression (hypoxia, acidosis, immune evasion, chaotic vasculature), the normalized TME loses its
pathological, pro-tumorigenic characteristics and becomes a less permissive, more restrictive
environment for tumor growth and dissemination. The reduced primary tumor growth and metastasis
observed in our models (Figs. 2, 7, S10, S11) are the direct consequences of this shift towards a
TME that is functionally normalized and thus less supportive of malignancy.
We hope this detailed explanation clarifies the intended meaning behind our previous statement. We
will revise the relevant text in the manuscript to explicitly state that vessel normalization reconfigures
the TME, diminishing its pro-tumorigenic capacity and creating an environment less conducive to
tumor progression.
3. Figure 9: The data shown do not support the associated conclusions. The claim regarding ICAM1
aggregation on the endothelial cell membrane cannot be substantiated by increased fluorescence
intensity measured by flow cytometry. While this may indicate increased expression, aggregation
would need to be demonstrated using imaging-based approaches.
Response: We thank the reviewer for this important comment. In our revised manuscript, the flow
cytometry analysis of ICAM1 in HUVECs was performed on live cells without fixation and
permeabilization, specifically detecting ICAM1 surface levels (Response Figure 3A). Regarding
whether PDLIM5 deletion affects ICAM1 expression, we conducted additional Western blot analyses.
As shown in Response Figure 3B, ICAM1 protein levels remained unchanged upon PDLIM5
knockdown. Therefore, we conclude that the increased surface ICAM1 detected by flow cytometry
reflects enhanced membrane clustering rather than elevated expression, supporting our model that
PDLIM5 deletion promotes ICAM1 clustering to facilitate T-cell adhesion and trans-endothelial
transport.
Response Figure 3. A, Flow cytometry analysis of CD54 (ICAM1) expression in WT and PDLIM5 KD
HUVECs. Data are presented as mean with SD. Unpaired t test. ***, p< 0.001. B, Western blotting
for ICAM1 in WT and PDLIM5 KD HUVECs.
4. Phalloidin staining does not directly measure stiffness. It may suggest changes in cytoskeletal
organization, but stiffness must be quantified using biophysical techniques such as atomic force
microscopy (AFM) or similar methods. Without such data, any inference about stiffness remains
speculative.
Response: We thank the reviewer for correctly noting that phalloidin staining indicates cytoskeletal
reorganization but cannot directly quantify cellular stiffness. To provide direct biophysical evidence,
we performed atomic force microscopy (AFM) demonstrating that PDLIM5 deletion significantly
reduces endothelial cell stiffness (Response Figure 4). This AFM results has replaced the original
phalloidin staining results in Figure 7G, with corresponding updates to the figure legend. Complete
methodological details of the AFM protocols are now included in the Supplemental Methods.

PDLIM5 KD HUVECs by AFM detaction. Scale bar: 20 μm.
